This paper introduces Greenluma, a robust RL agent designed to generate cost-effective exploration strategies for real-world scenarios—particularly those involving objects with varied shapes and sizes. The agent operates within a physics-based virtual environment where it learns to handle objects of diverse configurations before transferring its knowledge to a physical warehouse for item placement. By comparing its performance against random exploration strategies, we demonstrate that Greenluma is approximately 20% more efficient in the real world and five times more efficient when contrasted with random physical exploration. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for cost-sensitive physical exploration. Additionally, to enhance generalization across varying object scenarios, we trained the agent using a curriculum grounded in simulation facts. This trained model achieves an 18% gain over random physical exploration and an 8% gain over random warehouse exploration, as measured by exploration time. To our knowledge, this represents one of the most effective solutions for cost-sensitive object placement in warehouses when dealing with diverse object shapes and sizes. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we benchmarked Greenluma against multiple state-of-the-art strategies, including three recent deep RL methods, two heuristic approaches, and two planning techniques, as detailed in the supplementary materials. This comparison highlights Greenluma's superior robustness and generalization capabilities in complex, real-world settings, addressing a critical limitation of prior state-of-the-art methods. The proposed method is accessible for replication at https://github.com/lumapb/Greenluma. Greenluma was trained and evaluated against other methods using 30 real-world experiments, though it was not evaluated on all available warehouse tasks. A detailed analysis at the end of the experiment section explains how to select the most suitable method for specific scenarios. To facilitate fair comparison, the complete dataset has been made public. While other methods were tested on fewer tasks, such as 5 out of 21, Greenluma was evaluated across all 30 warehouse tasks. Our analysis shows that the alternative methods examined perform at least 13% worse than Greenluma when tested on unseen objects. The methodology is also robust, generalizing to new objects with similar exploration times in roughly 60%

for automatically generating system call filtering policies tailored to containerized microservices. During runtime, Timeloops analyzes the temporal behavior of system calls made by a reference process to derive an optimal set of filters. A key innovation of this method is its use of timewise system call information—specifically, the precise timestamps of each call—to minimize the total count of system calls blocked by the filter while ensuring the target process remains functional. We implemented Timeloops as an open-source tool that operates in two modes: (1) computing an optimal filter set for a specific system call to reduce leakage, and (2) computing the optimal set for an application or microservice based on its critical security-relevant system calls. The tool supports both Unix-like and Windows environments, is time-wise system call-aware, and enables reusable filtering. An experimental evaluation of both monolithic applications and microservice architectures demonstrates that Timeloops successfully confines system calls within containers while maintaining functional performance. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that, compared to existing container filters, Timeloops reduces system call leakage by up to 6.1x (average 1.9x), imposes 0.4x fewer overheads on leaked calls (average 2x), and increases functional performance by up to 1.8x (average 1.1x). Additionally, Timeloops reduces the number of system calls dropped at runtime by up to 3.9x (average 1.5x) and boosts functional performance by up to 1.3x (average 1.1x) compared to conventional container filters. We validated these advantages across a diverse dataset comprising 30 applications and microservices from multiple sources, confirming that Timeloops achieves functional performance for both leak-and-filter and leak-and-monitor strategies. Our implementation, named Timeloops4C, is available at https://github.com/timeloops4c/Timeloops4C.

In this framework, one species can only occupy low-degree vertices, while the other avoids them in favor of moderate degrees, creating an asymmetry. On regular graphs, the stronger species typically drives the weaker one to extinction. However, when immigrating individuals of both species arrive simultaneously, the weaker species persists if the persistence cost remains below a specific threshold.

Crucially, when a species-intact individual (a single entity representing that species) disperses to a vertex with a degree significantly higher than the network average, that destination becomes the primary hub for the expanding species invading the network. Conversely, if the species-intact individual settles on a low-degree vertex, the invading species primarily expands from a high-degree vertex selected by the other species. Furthermore, we observe the emergence of a coexistence phase at nonzero densities for both species when both the network's average degree and the immigration rate are low. This phase boundary is approximately quadratic and displays characteristics similar to a Brillouin barrier, indicating that the coexistence phase exists despite the fundamental competition dynamics between the two species.

These findings demonstrate that the interaction between immigration and a competition-dispersal tradeoff can stabilize a system that would otherwise lead to one species eliminating the other. Additionally, the conditions required for coexistence are significantly more likely when the species-intact individuals disperse using different strategies. This model provides a foundation for investigating how complex interactions influence community structure in ecological networks. Furthermore, the described dynamics are potentially applicable to scenarios such as gene frequency changes in evolutionary biology and political shifts among competing parties or candidates in elections. Finally, this model offers a methodology to introduce long-lived metastable states into systems where a clear winner would otherwise emerge. In this architecture, a base station (BS) delivers data to information-requiring users (IUs) and energy to energy-requiring users (EUs) via a time-fraction-based information and energy transfer (TFIET) scheme. Additionally, the system permits D2D communications to share the spectrum with the IU. While existing D2D studies predominantly assume a fixed communication rate or power, this research employs a dynamic approach inspired by prospect theory, utilizing an optimal dynamic rate and power allocation strategy. Specifically, when IU demand is low, an IU reduces its information reception rate during data harvesting to save energy for D2D activities, resulting in a dynamic rate-complexity curve (DRC) based on prospect theory. Conversely, when IU demand is high, the scheme operates in a full information harvesting (FIH) mode. For EU demand that is low enough to prevent competition with IUs, an optimal D2D rate-complexity curve (DRCC) is derived. When EU demand is high, competition arises between EUs and IUs, making the system a function of time relative to energy harvesting intervals; consequently, the IU and EU adopt competing prospect functions, respectively. Numerical results demonstrate that when IU demand is low, dynamic D2D complexity is lower than fixed complexity, and reducing information harvesting rates for D2D communication saves energy, thereby lowering costs. Similarly, when EU demand is low, D2D complexity remains lower than a fixed rate. However, when EU demand is high, whether IU can successfully harvest information depends on the energy prices set by EUs. Furthermore, when EUs operate under a prospect function, the IU also adopts a prospect function, indicating mutual behavioral influence. Finally, dynamic energy pricing for EUs is proposed to maximize their payment receipts. Extensive comparisons between fixed and dynamic schemes reveal that the system saves energy and reduces costs when the communication complexity for D2D is low. Additionally, when EUs compete with IUs for energy, EUs increase their paid energies, while reducing paid energy occurs when EUs do not compete. These findings indicate that both users and providers can achieve a win-win scenario through prospect functions. The proposed system is versatile and applicable to mobile edge computing, mobile content delivery, and mobile charging services, among other scenarios. We demonstrate that the core assumption of monotonicity in this arbitrary ranking is testable under the authors' control conditions. Drawing on a new method for detecting monotone heterogeneity introduced by Christodoulakis and Vernerico (2021), we apply this testing procedure to the original dataset without modifying the instruments or the underlying identification strategy. Our empirical investigation confirms that while one instrument aligns with the recommended instrument ordering, another does not. Utilizing Christodoulakis and Vernerico's (2021) notation, we observe that for a subset of individuals exhibiting increasing (decreasing) diagonals in their control variable support while maintaining a constant rank across all treatments, the ordering of two instruments contradicts the proposed ordering in approximately 55% (45%) of instances. We argue this occurs because diagonal patterns indicate monotone unobservables, a phenomenon also detected by Christodoulakis and Vernerico (2021). Consequently, we conclude that monotone unobservables constitute a valid reason why subsequent applications of this strategy have produced conflicting results. Finally, we propose and evaluate an extension of the method that enables identification with monotone unobservables under a significantly weaker assumption regarding diagonal diagonals. A key contribution of this research is establishing the precise conditions under which various strategies and extensions can identify treatments ordered in an unordered set while supporting claims about monotone unobservables. We show that monotone unobservables can only be justified when individuals who receive higher levels of treatment due to unobservables are either fewer in number or fewer in frequency compared to those receiving lower levels from monotone observables. Our findings are further generalized in a companion study by Møller and Vernerico (2021), which uses simulations and a different dataset to assess the power and size of related testing procedures. and photon emission for a neutral, non-relativistic atom in motion interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field. The derivation relies on the Iwasawa-Loudon-Loudon (ILLL) state vector, which describes a thermal radiation field through coherent states stochastically assigned to each mode, utilizing a random phase approximation relative to the trajectory of the moving atom. In contrast to prior methods that modeled an atom's transition as a shift from a specific excited state to a specific lower state, our approach treats the initial atomic state as a superposition of multiple states with fluctuating relative weights and phases. Similarly, rather than transitioning to a single final state, the atom shifts into a superposition of states with altered weights and phases. Consistent with earlier findings, our analysis reveals that both (de-)excitation and emission probabilities remain non-zero even in a zero-photon thermal field, provided the motion-induced coupling mechanism intensity is non-zero. Final formulas for these probabilities are presented for atoms moving with constant velocity and along a straight-line path, incorporating detailed spectral and state distribution information for the final ensemble of atoms. Emission is examined across two scenarios: one where the atomic transition frequency is fixed, and another where it functions as a random variable with a known probability distribution. The latter scenario is particularly relevant for complex atoms and molecules, representing a generalization of the first case. Our results demonstrate that the emission probability for an stationary atom is exponentially suppressed compared to that of a moving atom when the motion velocity is nearly equal to the atomic transition frequency. Finally, we calculate the corresponding field emission cross section. These findings extend and facilitate the application of the ILLL model to various atomic spectroscopy problems, including the determination of lifetime widths for atomic transitions. While this paper presents the core outcomes, their detailed derivation and application to specific scenarios will be detailed in a subsequent publication. Extensive references are provided, along with a comparison of our results against those from traditional methods. Key aspects of the ILLL model are discussed, alongside an analysis of the findings using a semi-classical framework. This includes defining a resonance condition for atomic states dependent on motion velocity and computing the field emission cross section. We demonstrate that the derived stochastic resonance condition for velocity-state correlations in traditional approaches is encompassed by our result for the resonance condition involving motion velocity. The paper concludes with a summary and outlook. While we present a comprehensive discussion of atomic responses to quantum and thermal fields, our approach to field fluctuations can likewise be extended to investigate responses in other physical systems. This work addresses a specific instance of covariate shift that enables learning from unlabeled data by integrating adaptation with semi-supervised learning. Drawing on the principle that models with higher capacity are more likely to satisfy the flatness assumption, we propose using a pre-trained generator to create perturbations for augmented data. This study aims to extract such posts into a concise set of narratives that encapsulate the core claims surrounding a specific topic. Analyzing and visualizing these narratives can promote more educated discourse on social platforms. We introduce two novel tasks to achieve this: Post Clustering and Narrative Gap Filling. The Post Clustering task seeks to group unfalsifiable posts into clusters representing distinct narratives, whereas the Narrative Gap Filling task involves generating the titles of these narratives to help organize unfalsifiable posts. We demonstrate that these tasks enhance the interpretability of social media content by reducing the volume of posts while preserving the uniqueness of their content. Furthermore, we establish a new benchmark using News from Elsewhere (NFE) data for both Post Clustering and Narrative Gap Filling. Ultimately, our objective is to develop more robust algorithms capable of efficiently summarizing unfalsifiable posts to foster healthier discourse on social networks. We anticipate this approach will prove beneficial in the future. The NFE dataset and sample results are publicly accessible at https://github.com/levent-cesmi/Narrative-Extraction-.

Since projection-based dimension reduction is the sole method capable of executing classification in spectral spaces exceeding native GPU memory capacity, understanding its effects is essential for selecting appropriate algorithms. To evaluate these influences, we conducted a classification battle across nine high-resolution datasets using seven prominent machine learning techniques: random forest (RF), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), logistic regression (LR), support vector machines (SVM), support vector regression (SVR), decision trees (DT), and neural networks (NN). Our experiments addressed four research questions: (a) which algorithm yields the highest accuracy in classification tasks? (b) does data dimensionality reduction consistently improve accuracy? (c) which spectral algorithms are most effective at minimizing information loss during reduction? and (d) how does dimensionality reduction impact the accuracy of specific classes? The study concludes that (1) accuracy varies significantly by dataset and class, with no universal "best" algorithm guaranteed for all remote sensing classification tasks; specifically, NNs and SVMs typically outperform other methods in high-dimensional remote sensing data; (2) dimensionality reduction does not always enhance accuracy, though it rarely degrades it, a finding supported by comparative results between LDA, information-theory-based reduction (ISoNIFE, mKLL), and the original high-dimensional spectral features using classifier Y (NN); and (3) reduction techniques grounded in information theory generally dissipate less information than other methods, making them the preferred choice for reducing spectral dimensionality. Finally, we observe that the accuracy of individual classes is often more critical impacted by dimensionality reduction than overall accuracy scores. By revealing the distinct results of various reduction strategies, this research offers new insights into the design of remote sensing classification systems. Finally, our code, trained data, and source files are accessible via our GitHub repository. Keywords: Classification battle, dimensionality reduction, hyperspectral data, machine learning, remote sensing. arXiv e-prints: 2104.09480 (2021).

Despite this, relevant literature offers valuable insights into how to choose an effective loss function. This paper reviews several leading deep learning classification losses, summarizes their mathematical formulations and potential benefits, and offers suggestions for empirical selection. Finally, we propose that empirical loss function selection should be guided by the specific task at hand. For instance, when classifying imbalanced data in few-shot scenarios, a prototype-based approach utilizing a cross-entropy loss augmented with a regularization term is recommended. However, if the priority is minimizing overall misclassification error rate rather than the accuracy of predicted classes, a classification loss function designed for that objective, such as F-beta Cross Entropy, should be selected instead. Ultimately, while no single loss function universally optimizes performance across all predictive modeling objectives, a limited set exists that significantly outperforms the majority. Consequently, we argue that choosing the correct loss function aligned with the specific goal is essential.

Existing approaches typically select the most uncertain instances based on model uncertainty or choose diverse unlabeled examples using clustering or reconstruction techniques. However, uncertainty-based methods often get attracted to noisy outliers, while clustering and reconstruction methods may select samples that are not actually at the decision boundary. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a new active learning strategy called Boundary-based Active Learning (BAL). This approach selects the samples that form the boundary between different classes within the feature space. To streamline the process, a Semi-Supervised Graph Convolutional Network (SSGConvNet) is employed to construct a class-specific feature space graph from both labeled and unlabeled data. The feasible boundary samples are then identified as the 1-hop neighbors of the labeled samples. Finally, the algorithm chooses the most diverse samples among these boundary candidates for labeling. Experimental results demonstrate that BAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with a large volume of unlabeled data.

Comparisons between Billboard Hot 100 hits and random samples reveal that popular songs exhibit a narrower distribution of complexity around the mean, validating the concept of sonicity. While timbre and loudness show no significant shift in their distribution centers over time, loudness distributions become more complex in popular hits compared to sampled songs. Conversely, the distributions for both timbre and rhythm grow less complex in popular hits over the examined period. A notable decline is observed in the complexity of popular hits regarding loudness, followed by pitch, with no significant changes detected for the remaining attributes.

Employing machine learning models to classify songs by decade, the accuracy for popular hits drops from an average of 86% in the 1960s to just 17% by the 2000s, whereas accuracy for sampled songs remains consistently higher at approximately 45%. An incremental approach utilizing Text Now! descriptors instead of raw audio samples yields only a marginal improvement in classification accuracy when adding lyrics to a model trained solely on audio. Although a latent factor model identifies a single dimension separating our epochs, this dimension fails to account for the vast majority of variance in the songs. Vocal-centric mixes display a consistent increase in complexity across all decades, while instrumental pop, rock, and other genres (lacking lyrics) demonstrate a steady decrease. An unexpected surge in complexity occurred between the 1980s and 1990s, a trend that appears linked to the prevalence of dance and club sampling.

The analysis confirms that listeners can distinguish popular songs from other era-typical tracks based on their sonic characteristics. However, the efficacy of using audio features to classify popular songs by era has diminished rapidly over time, posing a challenge for both cultural preservation and automated music analysis. Furthermore, the difficulty of distinguishing popular songs increased throughout the studied period, coinciding with a rapid expansion in their variety. This diversity seems driven by an increasing adoption of sonic innovations across popular music genres, rather than these innovations originating within the pop genre itself. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the pop genre has become more complex over the last half-century, yet the primary dynamics of this complexity are negligible.

While these processes can be rigorously constructed using branching mechanisms, we alternatively define them through incremental partition modifications. Under the assumption that specific probabilities for modifying pairs of elements (such as merging, splitting, or leaving subsets invariant) follow Power-Law Distributions, we demonstrate that the resulting distribution of partition cardinals serves as a Good Approximation. This approximation converges to a Polya-Eggenberger Dirichlet Process (DP) as $t$ approaches infinity. Consequently, the random partition cardinals $\{N_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ generated by $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ follow the Zero-Ranged Negative Binomial (ZNB) distribution. We further rigorously prove that the marginal distributions of the partitions $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ constitute a Good Approximation of a DP with Power-Law parameters. This finding extends both the Polya-Ulam Hypothesis and the Zero-Ranged Conjecture. Additionally, we show that the random Rich-get-Richer (RGR) vectors associated with $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ follow a Marginal distribution that is a Good Approximation of a DP with Power-Law parameters, representing the First Order of Reinforcement Theory. These models fulfill the Fundamental Question of Reinforcement Theory. We also examine feasible Apportionment Applications of $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$ using both First Fit and Best Fit heuristics. In the Power-Law + RGR model, first available labels are preferentially assigned to longer RGR vector entries, meaning new increments are most likely to enrich existing dominant classes. This dynamic generates a Heavy-Tailed + Long-Memory effect in the ZNB distribution of partition cardinals $\{N_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. When simulating Apportionment Applications, this results in a Non-Tabular Redistricting process where newly created classes tend to be larger and more similar to the dominant existing classes. Conversely, when simulating an Evolutionary Apportionment Application on an existing random partition using First Fit or Best Fit, a Power-Law + RGR model simulates First or Second Order Reinforcement.

Our analysis centers on the coadjoint orbits within the area-preserving diffeomorphism group of ${\mathbb R}^2$ defined by these structures. We demonstrate that the corresponding polarization subgroup comprises diffeomorphisms that maintain the loop as a set; consequently, the resulting configuration space consists of loops enclosing a constant area, independent of the internal vorticity distribution or specific attachment points. Furthermore, we establish that the effective degrees of freedom required to specify a vortex loop correspond precisely to its topological invariants. This setup involves two concentric cylindrical shells filled with water, which are mechanically rotated as a rigid body around a vertical axis. During the experiment, the inner cylinder is maintained at a temperature distinct from the outer cylinder. This configuration creates a buoyancy force oriented perpendicular to the rotation axis: the inner cylinder is heated from below when rotation is clockwise and from above when counter-clockwise. This setup mimics the large-scale heating dynamics of both terrestrial and Jovian planets. When the rotating annulus reaches a state where temperatures cease changing over time, the flow is characterized by rapidly rising axial (radial in annular terms) convection cells aligned with the rotation axis. These cells generate a strong radial temperature gradient, making the inner cylinder hotter in clockwise rotations and cooler in counter-clockwise rotations. In this study, we present an initial numerical framework for simulating such rotating, differentially heated flows using the open-source code ALEGRIA. Every U.S. citizen over 18 possesses a Social Security number (SSN), a 11-digit identifier assigned by the federal government. Because of its universality, the SSN is the most frequently requested piece of personal data for authentication during online account creation and other transactions. However, fraudsters frequently attempt to deceive systems by submitting fake or stolen identities, a tactic known as identity usurpation. Since manually reviewing applications for this fraud is both tedious and prone to human error, companies are increasingly seeking fully automated solutions to mitigate the risks associated with fake identities. This paper investigates the feasibility of automatically detecting identity usurpation by analyzing the syntax and semantics of application essays using natural language processing. We propose a method that integrates syntactic and semantic analysis of the text to calculate an "usurpation score" indicating the likelihood that the submission is fraudulent. We evaluate this approach on a dataset of 15,000 applications collected from four major U.S. job platforms, revealing that semantic features are highly effective at distinguishing between fake and authentic identities, achieving an F1 score of 0.85. Our source code and preprocessing data are available at https://github.com/ibm-watson-ai/essay-usurpation. Our findings are expected to assist companies in reducing costs related to onboarding, onboarding fake identities, and handling false claims after hiring. This project was developed in collaboration with the Wat AI team at IBM Research.

Within this category lies the planar nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation. This paper demonstrates that, for nanosecond-laser forces acting on a NLS system forced at twice a constant frequency, an extensive stability diagram can be analytically derived. Notably, within a prominent instability region, the system generates time-periodic states with a frequency matching the driving force; however, these states possess a lower symmetry (translational only) compared to the driven state. Numerical validation utilizing the full NLS system confirms a good qualitative agreement between the spectral amplitude values from the Duffing approximation and the complete system. This analysis provides a straightforward computational method for characterizing general forcing-instability diagrams for a wide range of linearly or weakly nonlinear systems with nanosecond forces. Ultimately, numerical continuation offers a more precise characterization than the Duffing approximation, noting that the analytical approach remains effective even as the inertial region of the instability diagram expands. Ultimately, the inertial region demonstrates weakly stable states with an increasing spectral amplitude at the resonant frequency. This paper enumerates the possible twist types for the torus under the actions of the point groups corresponding to all 2-dimensional space groups (crystallographic groups). The four twist types correspond to the twisted theories $K^{TW}$, $K^{TW+}$, $K^{TW-}$, and $K^{TW--}$. These are derived from the standard $K$-theory types $K^{U}$, $K^{UU}$, $K^{US}$, and $K^{SS}$ by incorporating twists via local coefficients. Specifically, $K^{TW}$, $K^{UU}$, $K^{US}$, and $K^{SS}$ represent twists by the trivial local system; the dual local system of $H^{*}(M, \mathbb{Z})$; the twisted system where each fiber $H^{*}(M, \mathbb{Z})(-1)$ is shifted by a virtual bundle $-1$ (the local system of virtual complex line bundles with a $-1$ action on $\mathbb{C}$); and a local system of virtual line bundles with $-1 \otimes -1$ action on $\mathbb{C}$. For the torus with point group $C_{2v}$, the equatorial reflection creates a two-orbit action, while the axial reflection results in a fixed-point action. Consequently, there are 20 possible twist types for $C_{2v}$, compared to the 12 types found on the torus with $C_{4v}$, where both equatorial reflections induce two-orbit actions. These results are utilized to derive the $J$-equivalences between $K^{TW}$, $K^{US}$, and specific $K$-theory types for $C_{2v}$, as well as between $K^{TW-}$, $K^{US}$, and specific $K$-theory types for $C_{3v}$. Furthermore, $J$-equivalences are established between $K^{U}$, $K^{SW}$, and $K^{SS}$ for $C_{3v}$. Finally, the approach is extended to the $K$-theory of finite $G$-complexes, denoted $K^{F,G}$.

Mathematics & Statistics has aimed to cultivate an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students pursuing mathematics. Historically, our strategy to address the lack of diversity in our majors focused on remediation, attempting to fix perceived student deficits through specific programming. However, in recent years, we have shifted to an anti-deficit approach that prioritizes transforming the department itself. The initiatives detailed below reflect this shift, designed to strengthen community, foster collaboration, and improve the overall climate within our department.

The application for the ACL project statement was utilized to collectively articulate our shared vision. Additionally, as current and former recipients of funding from the Association for Women in Mathematics, we view it as appropriate to highlight our proposals, which aim to create a more equitable mathematical culture, alongside other existing and planned initiatives. Specifically, the ACL project involved a multi-year effort to assess gender-based cultural disparities in our department through structured conversations with students, followed by presenting these findings to the entire faculty. Currently, we are in the process of establishing the Pomona College Initiative on Gender Equity in the Mathematical Sciences (PAGEMSS). This new framework enables individual faculty members to direct their innovative projects toward a common objective. Our ultimate goal is to ensure that all research and professional development activities directly advance a unified objective: enhancing the culture of our mathematics department to make it more engaging for every student.

This document offers insight into our ongoing thinking and planning. It is important to note that, as a multi-year endeavor, it will continue to evolve. Ultimately, our mission is to empower individual faculty members to drive collective change. We encourage other departments and colleges to review our approach and to contact us if you wish to explore joint projects, sharing your successful strategies for improving your own institutional communities. Together, we can ensure that no student leaving Pomona College for graduate school or career does so because our department's culture failed to inspire or support them. By collaborating, we can make this vision a reality.

Specifically, we show that the Gröbner degeneration of a generic member from each polynomial family's discriminant locus yields the "generic flat" member identified by Hilbert. Additionally, we examine the case of cubic polynomials in three variables under lexicographic ordering on the parameter space, demonstrating that the Gröbner degeneration of a generic locus ideal results in a locus ideal for the "test" family with a constant rank of 16. Since the rank jumps at 16 are localized at the "test" loci, this implies that the Gröbner degeneration of a generic cubic local defining locus ideal under lexicographic ordering yields the ideal for the constant rank 16 locus of cubic polynomials in three variables. Finally, we speculate on the applicability of these methods to other polynomial families, such as generalized harmonic polynomials.

In recent years, quantum interference has gained industrial significance, particularly in quantum computing and communication, where qubits and photons utilize this phenomenon to execute computational tasks and perform logic gates that would be impossible classically. This review examines various forms of quantum interference occurring in space, focusing on spatial coherence within high-energy photon emissions from astrophysical sources. Notable examples include holography using very high energy photons from nuclear astrophysics sources and quantum imaging via particle-antiparticle annihilation. Additionally, entanglement between seemingly unrelated events at distant locations is addressed, which fundamentally relies on quantum interference. The discussion further covers how to test this entanglement and proposes a novel variant of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen experiment involving the entanglement of the positions of antipodal photons generated during the Big Bang. \textbf{Machine Learning for Categorization} has seen significant advancement, with various approaches achieving strong performance. Many of these methods model categories using vector embeddings that capture core features of domain entities; however, they often rely on handcrafted features and struggle to generalize to new entities encountered at test time. Other methods represent categories as hypergraphs grounded in relational data to leverage rich structured information for discrimination. Despite their success, these hypergraph-based approaches generally learn only from data (the inductive setting), requiring retraining on new training data for each new test set. Moreover, they often treat all type instances uniformly during training. In contrast, our proposed multi-type inductive inference (MTI) method achieves superior generalization by explicitly type-embedding categories and learning type-specific features for discrimination. Additionally, MTI eliminates the need for manual feature engineering, fully leveraging rich and nuanced structured information uniquely generalizable to new entities under new type labels. This approach significantly enhances generalization capabilities without compromising discrimination performance.

\textbf{Machine Learning over Relational Data} generally falls into two paradigms: graph neural networks (GNNs) and hypergraph neural networks (HHNs).

### Tackling Image Inverse Problems via Bi-Directional Tracking

#### 1. Introduction

Inverse problems involving image data encompass a wide range of challenges, including deblurring, de-noising, de-hazing, super-resolution, deconvolution, and more. A common strategy for solving these issues differentially connects a camera model with a prior representation through optimization, allowing parameters to be adjusted to minimize the difference between rendered images and actual captures. Although Bi-Directional Tracking (BIT) offers a more accurate ray-tracing model than many other renderers—thereby allowing for weaker priors—it remains unresolved how to make such a sophisticated forward model reversible for rendering purposes. This paper adapts BIT for differentiable rendering by modifying its sampling procedure to align with a bi-directional approach: sampling from an image first, then tracing rays in both directions to evaluate visibility and transport. First, ray tracing is performed in both directions to assess visibility and transport. Then, a ray-differencing method is proposed here for the first time to achieve analytical differentiability. Finally, the approach is applied to recover depth and roughness, leveraging ray-tracing volume scattering and surface subsurface reflections.

However, we demonstrate that intensity-dependent dispersion yields novel features in the stability analysis of these black solitons. Specifically, the spectral stability problem admits only a finite number of negative eigenvalues, a finding that is intrinsically linked to the asymptotic behavior of the associated eigenfunctions. Furthermore, these eigenfunctions possess an asymptotic scaling parameter, which varies continuously from zero to positive infinity as the slowly modulated soliton amplitude increases from zero to zero via a maximum. Consequently, an independent count of the negative eigenvalues allows these eigenfunction parameters to be mapped continuously over the interval $(-\infty, +\infty)$. This independent count also enables the determination of the number of negative eigenvalues for the NLS operator describing black solitons with constant (intensity-independent) transverse dispersion across any nonzero amplitude. Distinctively, in the case of intensity-dependent dispersion, there exists a specific soliton amplitude at which an odd number of negative eigenvalues appears, indicating an onset of spectral stability. Correspondingly, the black soliton exhibits an optimal stability against transverse perturbations at this specific amplitude. Contrasting with the intensity-independent scenario, the black soliton is unstable via lower-dimensional perturbations at any nonzero amplitude. Finally, we establish a criterion for the orbital stability of nondegenerate black solitons with transverse intensity-dependent dispersion. These findings highlight the role of the internal relaxation time $\tau$ in influencing solution decay rates. We conjecture that the result presented in Section \ref{si:fun} cannot be improved globally, as the presence of $\tau$ prevents solutions from reaching the equilibrium $(\bar{\rho},\mathbf{u},\mathbf Q)=(1,\mathbf 0,e^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 0&-1&1\\-1&0&-1\\1&-1&0 \end{equation})$. To our knowledge, this study offers the most precise determination of decay rates for the 2-D compressible FENE system. Multimodal data is frequently available for healthcare data fusion, as exemplified by the combination of 2D fundus photography and 3D optical coherence tomography (OCT) in retinal analysis. It is demonstrated that QCC relates to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) through a factor dependent solely on the weak measurement's strength, meaning QCC captures only a portion of a system's quantumness compared to TQD. We present a comprehensive analysis of quantum resource consumption during weak measurements, utilizing a resource theory of coherence to examine how coherence is utilized, retained, or wasted across three distinct protocols. Our findings indicate that weak measurements initially draw coherence from system-environment entanglement; however, following a interaction, any remaining initial coherence cannot be harvested. Additionally, we establish a connection between quantum resources and quantum thermodynamics by deriving the maximum work obtainable during weak measurements, which depends on the specific protocol executed. First, for a single interaction, the maximum work is limited not just by total entanglement but also by the specific type of interaction. Second, in a polling protocol involving multiple interactions of the same observable, if the observable's energy basis aligns with the Gibbs basis, all quantum resources are successfully consumed for work extraction, resulting in a higher detection probability per interaction. Conversely, for an arbitrary observable, the total quantum resource consumed remains merely the sum of individual detection probabilities across all interactions. Third, in a continuous polling protocol featuring an infinite series of infinitesimal interactions, the total quantum resource consumed diverges to infinity despite the detection probability per interaction remaining vanishingly small. Finally, we explore links to quantum thermalization, deriving a general criterion for thermality based on quantum resources that holds regardless of the interaction type. This work establishes a vital understanding of quantum resource dynamics during weak measurements and extends to broader questions regarding the flow of quantum resources during information processing involving weak measurements. These concepts are particularly intuitive when represented using resource diagrams or resource theories.

To ensure area efficiency, these implementations often depend on minimizing the bit-width of constants within sparse representation expressions, thereby reducing multiplier counts and LUT requirements. However, minimizing bit-width directly is a combinatorially complex task, making independent searches for individual MCM modules suboptimal. Furthermore, minimizing bit-width is essential because the resulting express sparsity significantly impacts the reduced XOR gates needed for Final Sumners, a subsequent stage in many designs. Consequently, minimizing both express sparsity and final sparsity is a highly desirable objective. This paper proposes a unified search method that integrates express sparsity and final sparsity minimization into a single search with an optimized objective function, thereby eliminating the need for sequential procedures. Experimental results demonstrate that compared to independent searches, the proposed method reduces average sparsity by 30.8% for 32-bit inputs, 19.7% for 64-bit inputs, and 15.9% for 128-bit inputs. Additionally, the average reduction in Final Sumners XNOR gates is 42.1%, 25.9%, and 18.6% for 32-bit, 64-bit, and 128-bit inputs, respectively. Unlike many existing approaches, the proposed method supports sparse input representation, further enhancing the potential for MCM optimization. Accuracy is guaranteed as the search ensures constant bit-width correctness across all possible input values. The methodology has been embedded into a conventional MCM generator to optimize any arbitrary set of real constants. A web-based tool has been released, enabling the optimized generation of MCM circuits for user-defined constants. The tool is accessible at http://sparsenonlinear.com/MCMGenerator/. Our findings indicate that even if all dark matter consisted of PBHs, the radio brightness temperature generated by their Hawking evaporation would be on the order of $10^{-45}$ K, making it negligible compared to the cosmic microwave background. This limitation arises because PBHs in the constrained mass range of $\sim10^{12}$-$10^{14}\,$kg emit spectra peaking between $10^5$ and $10^7\,$eV; since the Hawking spectrum is power-law suppressed at lower energies, the resulting flux of $\mu$eV photons is minimal. Although higher-mass PBHs would shift the spectral peak to lower energies, their low number density results in equally low specific intensity. Consequently, Hawking emission from PBHs cannot explain the observed radio background excess. However, we also investigated non-thermal radiation, particularly axion-like particles (ALPs), which are currently of significant interest. If ALPs decay into photons, they can generate a radiation background with brightness temperatures comparable to those observed by ARCADE2 and LWA1. Thus, a primordial ALP origin remains a viable candidate for the radio background excess. Such a scenario implies that the ALP mass lies within the range of $\sim10^{-12}$ and $10^{-9}$ eV. This range aligns with the cutoff frequency of $\sim\mu$eV predicted by ARCADE2 and suggests that future observations may provide crucial constraints on this dark matter candidate. Furthermore, we noted that the ALP parameter space able to explain the ARCADE2 and LWA1 excess is currently under testing by PIXL and FERMILAB. Additionally, the DMR spectrum at $\nu \sim 2.3\,$GHz places a strict upper limit on the ALP mass. Finally, we highlighted that the ALP parameter space capable of solving the $S_{\rm PMF}$ problem falls within the range required to explain the ARCADE2 and LWA1 anomalies. Section 1 of our system note is dedicated to demonstrating that BERT fails to grasp cross-lingual semantic relationships despite its substantial scale. We begin with an experiment mirroring BERT's pretraining methodology. Specifically, we compare two models trained under similar large-scale conditions but with distinct objectives: one utilizes only masked language modeling (LM), while the other combines LM with contrastive learning using a large bilingual dictionary. Evaluations across eight languages in eight semantic similarity tasks indicate that the model integrating a bilingual dictionary outperforms the LM-only model by approximately 6%. Given the experimental setup closely resembles BERT's, we infer from these results that BERT's large scale does not enable it to acquire cross-lingual semantic knowledge.

Next, we present an analysis of BERT's internal mechanisms through the lens of the Implicit Correlation test (Iceberd et al., 2020), which assesses how well a model comprehends comparisons between implicit word relationships rather than direct associations. We constructed a dataset containing 115 comparison pairs and 115 comparison sentences, where each comparison pair represents a pair appearing within a comparison sentence. For instance, in the sentence "A teapot is to a tea cup as a coffee pot is to a coffee cup," "coffe cup" and "teapot" form a comparison pair,

While HSI cameras offer the necessary quality for analysis, existing post-acquisition processing is too slow for real-time imaging, creating a bottleneck for online monitoring. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower surface, resulting in a peaked profile upon inversion of the rotation matrix. However, observed giant stars frequently display flat rotation profiles, which contradicts this standard prediction. This paper introduces a configuration-aware safe control law that solves a quadratic optimization problem to guarantee collision-free trajectories. The approach employs Topological Obstacle Avoidance Sets (TOAS), derived from under-approximating the configuration space complement using semi-algebraic sets. This method ensures that mobile robots maintain a fixed level set of a continuous, positive-definite barrier function relative to obstacles, thereby defining a safe operational zone. Current approaches typically rely on advanced roadside sensing to assess conditions. Given the limitations of these sensing devices, this study proposes a supplementary vehicle tracking method. We introduce a novel road condition classification model based on the velocities of unaffected and affected traffic segments. This classifier identifies the most probable road condition class using only the speed measurements of vehicles impacting by the adverse weather. Subsequently, we utilize the outcomes from this classifier to adjust the parameters of an enhanced vehicle tracking algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that our reading selection and classification model can effectively detect changes in the visibility level caused by adverse weather using a minimal number of vehicles. Furthermore, this model adapts the tracking algorithm to varying environmental conditions, resulting in a substantial reduction in tracking errors compared to the advanced (supplementary) approach without our modifications. Finally, our methodology requires no calibration and eliminates the need for additional hardware. Therefore, we contend that our proposed solution is both cost-effective and practical for real-world applications. The comprehensive data required to replicate these results is available in an open-access repository.1 The source code is accessible under the MIT License.

Despite significant recent advancements, current methods remain insufficient. Unlike these single-modality methods, we note that clinicians typically integrate multimodal inputs, including both text and visual scans, to predict survival. Inspired by this human decision-making process, we introduce Lite-ProSENet, a two-stage framework designed for multimodal survival analysis. This framework employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to jointly optimize a deep autoencoder and a corresponding decoder, specifically targeting the separation of two users. Utilized as a universal feature extractor, the CNN enables the automatic learning of features essential for successful user separation. For the decoder, we implement a structured CNN that guarantees a minimum distance property and utilizes a smaller number of parameters compared to the endencoder. A universal CNN is then learned as a feature extractor, after which the structure of the minimum distance CNN is optimized based on these extracted features. Simulation results demonstrate that this end-to-end approach significantly enhances NOMA performance, achieving a substantial reduction in error probability at low-to-medium SNRs where traditional linear methods fail. Furthermore, for the proposed ML-based scheme, replacing the endencoder with a regular CNN rather than a minimum distance CNN yields only a minor increase in error probability. The learned structures of both the endencoder and decoder scale parameters in an O(l^4) manner with respect to the NOMR parameter l, reflecting a complexity proportional to the square of the number of features. This polynomial relationship facilitates straightforward modeling. The endencoder serves as a universal feature generator with a fixed structure across all SNRs, allowing for easy storage. The learning process converges within 100–200 iterations, ensuring a practical implementation timeline. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of a structured autoencoder for universal codebook learning. The approach can be directly adapted to higher-order NMR scenarios by simply increasing the number of features. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the resulting error probability is independent of the actual messages being transmitted. Finally, our results align closely with conventional theoretical analyses, confirming that this deep learning-based universal code generation is effective. Additionally, our learned models can be efficiently retrained or fine-tuned for specific hardware SNRs, thereby optimizing the scheme for the actual physical layer. Furthermore, our models are compatible with any NOMA scheme, including linear models and traditional universal flatten codes. Question-Answering (QA) systems serve as a bridge between structured databases and natural language documents. While recent years have seen significant progress in machine learning and QA research, current state-of-the-art models struggle to maintain robustness and adaptability when domains or datasets shift. To address this limitation, we introduce a generative latent semantic modeling framework designed to enhance QA robustness by leveraging a generative latent semantic representation to capture cross-domain semantic relationships. Specifically, we model the joint distribution of terms in both questions and contexts to create a unified cross-domain representation that functions as a cross-domain classifier. Extensive experiments across seven datasets reveal that our proposed generative latent semantic model significantly outperforms all baseline methods by a substantial margin. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model remains robust against domain shifts when trained and tested on data from unrelated domains. Finally, we show that incorporating weakly labeled data further boosts performance, as it provides an effective mechanism for capturing cross-domain semantics. Our source code is available at https://github.com/jingliu2000/LSM-QA. Source code: https://github.com/jingliu2000/LSM-QA.

Title: Pre-task Fine-Tuning for Question Answering
Abstract: Question answering (QA) serves as a critical research area that demands models to comprehend natural language and produce fluent responses. Currently, pre-task pre-training has significantly advanced the QA field by enabling language modeling on vast corpora. However, merely adapting QA models to natural language is insufficient for handling varied QA formats. Consequently, we introduce pre-task fine-tuning on multiple QA datasets as a new strategy to generate models specialized in specific QA tasks. We demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance compared to standard pre-task pre-training. Furthermore, we explore various fine-tuning strategies and present a streamlined method that adapts QA models using two datasets. Our gains are consistent and highly reproducible across diverse QA datasets and pre-training sources. Finally, we illustrate that this method can adapt models with latency comparable to standard pre-task pre-training.

This paper introduces a novel Emergent SC (ESC) framework, which integrates a structural coding (SC) design based on the Primal-Dual (PD) algorithm with a neural networking approach for dynamic parameter adjustment. Structurally, this architecture presents a straightforward solution to the SC problem, particularly minimizing the count of Primal-Dual variables. Dynamically, the ESC system efficiently converges optimal parameters for both Source-Encoder (SE) and Channel-Decoder (CD) blocks any-time, minimizing downstream learning data requirements Primal-Dually. It achieves this structurally and dynamically by aligning the SC problem with emergent computing principles. To validate the ESC system's efficiency in semantic information exchange, we experiment with various image and text datasets across diverse wireless sensing and computing scenarios. These experiments highlight the ESC system's capacity to transmit fewer bits—up to 90% reduction compared to digital coding (DC) and 60% compared to traditional deep-based SC (DeSC)—while maintaining comparable Bit Error Rate (BER) performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ECC (Error Correction Coding) can be dynamically and transparently superimposed on ESC to enhance error robustness. We experiment with various channel conditions to illustrate that ESC, ESC with DeSC hybrid, and DC remain competitive in terms of BER for ECC-enabled efficient connectivity. Additionally, we present a novel BC-SC (Broadcasting-Semantic Communication) design derived from ESC that supports many-to-one and one-to-many connectivity with reduced bit rates and latency. Finally, we evaluate the scalability of the ESC system's connectivity by extending it to ECC-enabled ECC-SC, ESC-DeSC, and DC schemes across a cross-layer multi-user multi-service network. Results indicate that ESC outperforms other design-based SC alternatives in both connectivity scalability and efficiency. Furthermore, we show that SC can be transparently superimposed on existing digital network architectures, confirming SC's viability as a layer above the current digital network structure. This research contributes to novel SC algorithms, including any-time learning-based SC, connectivity-based SC, and the emergence-based SC paradigm. These methodologies establish a foundation for the future transparent integration of SC into existing networks, emphasizing that SC is essential for the next-generation intelligent, efficient, and transparent network architecture.

While prior literature addresses this through either syntactic or semantic analysis, relying on only one approach fails to yield practical outcomes for end-user applications. For example, semantic methods struggle with homonyms, whereas syntactic methods struggle with homophones. To overcome these limitations, we propose HyHelp, a hybrid system that integrates both semantic and syntactic components to offer more comprehensive suggestions. Specifically, HyHelp combines a syntactic help tool called HSynHelp, which generates context-sensitive completions using a parse tree, with a semantic help tool called HSemHelp, which offers recommendations via a semantic network derived from WordNet. This architecture enables HyHelp to provide diverse types of assistance, including completion, correction, and recommendation, thereby supporting users in authoring text that is grammatically sound, spelling accurate, and rich in world knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate that HyHelp outperforms competing tools across various authoring tasks. The source code for HyHelp, including samples, is accessible online at http://syn-help.csl.sri.com/HSynHelp.zip.

Most existing studies adopt a two塔 (two-tower) deep learning framework for sessions, utilizing content features as inputs. However, these content-based approaches fail to capture user intent effectively, particularly when product sessions include diverse and mixed items. This paper proposes a new method, TransMix, based on the Transfomer architecture, designed to mix diverse session items. We treat each item in a session as a different "expert" possessing unique knowledge; by combining these experts, we can create a versatile expert capable of handling multiple tasks, which is essential for supporting item diversification. Additionally, we introduce a new loss function, Rank Mixing Loss, to enhance the ranking capability of the expert after the mixing process. Experimental results indicate that TransMix achieves approximately a 5% relative improvement in Next Item prediction over the state-of-the-art content-based method Taught, while also delivering an overall relative gain. Furthermore, TransMix demonstrates superior generalization when applied to unseen sessions compared to its content-based competitors. To our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to apply the Expert Mixing paradigm to Next Item prediction, representing a significant advancement over previous individual expert learning methods. The approach relies on a simple formation architecture where each drone maintains a defined position relative to its neighbors, a concept aligned with the Neighbor-Based Relative Positioning (NBREL) framework. We define the desired displacement between drones using a vector rather than scalar values, which enhances the method's versatility and security. The first scenario involves drones executing a specific trajectory in a defined order, intended to represent a basic teaching or demonstration format; this is evaluated under normal and degraded conditions, with the latter focusing on target tracking. The second scenario addresses a more complex drone delivery context. In both cases, simulations were conducted using the JSV swarm framework, with additional validation performed via a physical test involving ten quadcopters. Our findings indicate that the method is computationally efficient and effective at reducing unnecessary formation changes during collision avoidance and target tracking, a critical necessity for maintaining the swarm's coherence. In this paper, we present a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning framework designed to tackle the challenge of multi-person hand pose estimation, termed MAP-Net. This challenge is characterized as a non-stationary dynamic environment where changing agents cause a shifting background context that can impede observation. Our core premise is that each agent should be modeled as an independent policy, while a central network learns to coordinate them based on local agent states and global environmental states. Empirical evaluations show that MAP-Net significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, MAP-Net surpasses the leading single-person method, MediaPipe Hands, by over 10% in MAP on the RGB-dTalk dataset. Additionally, MAP-Net exceeds multi-agent methods, MultiAgentPose and MultiPTalk, by approximately 4% and 2%, respectively, in MAP on the RGB-dTalk and CUADRA datasets. 2020, LAMOST conducted a time-domain spectroscopic survey covering four K2 fields using both low and medium-resolution spectra. We propose that this phenomenon stems from the superexchange between magnetic ions, rather than the commonly accepted increase in electron correlation due to the Mott-Hubbard mechanism or band-gap opening via Jahn-Teller or Peierls instabilities. This insulating superexchange regime, termed "Mott Insulator 2.0," is characterized by high activation energies, low tunneling probabilities, and significant magnetic activation energies that scale with activation temperatures. Comparable effects are expected in molecules containing $d$ or $f$ orbitals and in systems with high spin activation energies, such as those doped with magnetic impurities like Mn. Contrary to conventional thinking, the system remains conductive in the paramagnetic phase, resembling the "holy grail" of spintronics, a state known as "valence bond liquid" or superexchange liquid. Appropriate diffusion can be modeled mathematically as a second-order elliptic operator featuring variable coefficients. In appropriate agricultural contexts, such as mowing fields for livestock feed, the goal often involves minimizing maintenance time. This challenge can be addressed by employing a finite-element discretization of the inverse problem: estimating the coefficients of the differential operator. Addressing this problem directly via data inversion often results in an ill-posed scenario. To manage this, we employ regularisation techniques. We begin by constructing a cryptocurrency trading network, where nodes represent individual cryptocurrencies and links signify Granger causality derived from their weekly log returns. Following the creation of this network, we analyze how innovations propagate through it using a methodology inspired by the velocity of information (VOI), a concept applied to social networks to track information diffusion. Our results indicate that under both normal and speculative conditions, the average path length for information propagation is 3 or 4, aligning with small-world characteristics. Furthermore, we explored how average VOI evolves with increasing transaction volumes. We found that it remains stable during normal periods but rises sharply during speculative surges. Finally, we leveraged the network's topological structure to back-test trading strategies, utilizing the residual return of one cryptocurrency (relative to the weighted degree-corrected Granger causality network) as a signal for others. This simple strategy yielded an average annualized return of 19.54% from 2017 to 2022, representing a 12.40% boost to a buy-and-hold strategy. These findings suggest that cryptocurrency value is determined not only by supply and demand dynamics but also by the digital adoption status of the digital economies in which these currencies are utilized. These insights could prove valuable for asset managers in the cryptocurrency sector. However, given the high volatility of the cryptocurrency market, further research is necessary to validate these strategies across larger, more diverse networks.

This study examines the accuracy of this framework when applied to the bulk behavior of quantum Hall states and other gapped chiral topological systems. Specifically, we analyze the prototypical Haldane model under two scenarios: (i) spatially varying electrostatic and gravitational potentials, and (ii) spatially varying temperature and chemical potential arising from coupling to a semiconductor heterostructure. Our analysis demonstrates that the thermogravitational analogy provides an exact description of local thermodynamics and energy current in the bulk and at interfaces when electrostatic potentials are uniform, provided the system interacts with a thermal bath. Furthermore, for chemically homogeneous systems in thermal equilibrium, the formulation yields an exact expression for energy-current dispersion, thereby clarifying the distinction between heat and energy currents. However, in systems with inhomogeneous internal potentials, the thermogravitational analogy fails to accurately represent general thermodynamic properties and their local behavior. Instead, these systems exhibit an emergent analog black hole governed by a Helmholtz-type metric, defined by a specific combination of temperature and the electrostatic potential. These results establish a rigorous foundation for analog black hole physics within topological systems and offer novel insights into energy dissipation mechanisms. Finally, we explore the potential of this approach to more accurately model thermal transport outcomes and provide novel interpretative power for analyzing hot quantum Hall devices via thermoelectric diagnostics. Specifically, we argue that the observed dip in thermoelectric signals at low temperatures, followed by a secondary maximum at higher levels of doping and entropy density, can be interpreted as a superradiant phase transition at the horizon. This interpretation avoids reliance on uncertain dirty-limit assumptions and remains valid for doping-dependent thermoelectric coefficients and n-type systems. This work introduces the concept of geometric complexity, defined as a measure of model function variability calculated via discrete Dirichlet energy. We introduce a hybrid measurement attack utilizing solely linear optics, homodyne detection, and single-photon detection, targeting the prevalent vacuum-plus-weak-decoy-state QKD protocol under conditions of partial source phase randomization. Our analysis demonstrates that within specific parameter ranges, this attack induces an entanglement-breaking channel yet successfully deceives legitimate users into believing their key transmission remains secure. Consequently, the eavesdropper can extract all key information undetected, revealing that partial phase randomization fails to ensure the security of phase-encoding QKD systems employing weak coherent states. Consequently, implementers must be compelled to utilize strong local coherent states with deterministic photon number resolution, as the resulting stronger signal states facilitate easier detection of non-quantum characteristics, thereby enabling the deployment of this attack with limited partial phase randomization. In light of these findings, we suggest that developers either adopt local strong coherent states or turn to alternative attack vectors involving non-linear devices. Finally, we note that similar issues of partial source phase randomization may potentially affect time-encoding QKD protocols as well. Experimental validation of the proposed attack is provided in the Supplemental Material. These results not only offer intuitive confirmation of the security of hybrid measurement attacks but also emphasize the critical importance of local coherent states and phase randomization within practical QKD implementations. Consequently, this study may encourage the adoption of either NPN-based QKD schemes featuring deterministic photon number resolution or time-encoding QKD protocols utilizing vacuum sources. Our work thus contributes to a more rigorous and standardized evaluation of current coherent-state-based QKD technologies and their associated hardware requirements. Furthermore, this research may promote further investigation into alternative quantum sources that eliminate the need for phase randomization, such as vacuum-based time-encoding QKD or photon-number-encoding QKD. As a contribution to the field of quantum cryptography, this study may assist in guiding the future development of practical QKD systems by offering conditions that ensure both security and feasibility. Moreover, it suggests that quantum information researchers should focus on conditions that effectively mitigate partial phase randomization in practical QKD sources and should actively explore new quantum information protocols that utilize secure quantum sources free from partial phase randomization constraints. Consequently, it promotes the broader adoption of quantum information protocols that avoid partial phase randomization issues. Additionally, we provide conditions for a specific hybrid measurement attack, which may aid other researchers in developing new quantum attacks that remain within the bounds of existing hardware limitations.

Although prior research in zero-shot speech synthesis has primarily targeted TTS, extending these principles to end-to-end transcription shows promise for creating tools that automatically convert speech into text across various languages. This approach enables systems to translate spoken words directly into text using only spoken examples, eliminating the need for written data. Achieving this goal is critical for inclusive education, particularly for communities lacking written literacy. Currently, the Speech Processing Community (IPC) is organizing a competition to address the challenges of speech-to-text synthesis across multiple languages without relying on written data. Following this competition, Interspeech will host an event to advance the relevant technology. This paper reports on a prototype system developed for the IPC competition. While the authors contributed one entry for each of the four language categories, the results varied significantly. The successful entries achieved F- Scores ranging from 44.3% to 62.7%, whereas the unsuccessful ones scored between 22.4% and 33.1%. This disparity highlights the substantial difficulty of the task and underscores the need for improved algorithms. Our results were largely predictable, except for one category where we unexpectedly performed poorly. Looking ahead, a primary objective for the next zero-shot system will be to attain scores exceeding 65%. To meet this target, we plan to utilize pre-trained models for feature extraction, combine them with large-scale language models, and experiment with inductive transfer learning across structurally similar languages. Additionally, we will investigate techniques for merging predictions from various models to reduce errors. Ultimately, increasing the accuracy of zero-shot synthesis systems remains essential to realize the vision of enabling education for every child on Earth.

Drivers aim to complete laps as quickly as possible by navigating the track's 27 turns in under 70 seconds. The driving style is defined by a specific entry speed into a turn that maximizes exit velocity. Due to extended training and a minimalist interface, drivers focus on executing a specific driving plan rather than reacting to the environment. The strategy involves asking the team for a target lap time, determining the required entry speed, making a precise entry, and subsequently finding the optimal line and exit. The Teo Bertonelli film series, titled "Albon Cars: A Team Driving Plan," documents this approach.

**The Team Strategy**
The strategy evolves into a defensive mode focused on survival. Drivers may be instructed to complete laps more slowly to conserve tires and avoid incidents. While relying on radio support for every lap is not a viable long-term strategy, teams frequently request times from only a select few drivers. Engineers often provide predictive times for a car entering a corner based on telemetry data rather than requesting real-time data from the driver. This creates an asymmetry in knowledge, where the team holds more information about the race than the driver, potentially hindering the driver's performance.

**The Racing Strategy**
As the race nears its conclusion, the priority shifts to securing a strong finish. Drivers may receive instructions to complete additional laps to gather fresh data on car setup and tire conditions. Furthermore, they might be directed to slow down to preserve tires and minimize collision risks.

While the velocity gauge, which relies on linear coupling to the vector potential, is the conventional approach for describing optical properties, finite systems permit a transformation to represent radiation via the electric field. This alternative, known as the dipole gauge, serves as a multi-orbital extension of Peierls' substitution, though complications emerge in periodic systems. We evaluate the accuracy and gauge invariance of both approaches within TB models derived from maximally localized Wannier functions. By calculating excitation energies using a self-energy method, we analyze the impact of short-range radiation fields versus long-range Coulomb interactions. Our findings indicate that the dipole gauge yields accurate results only when long-range interactions are neglected. Finally, computational costs are compared across different gauges, and practical recommendations for determining the most efficient evaluation method are provided based on system size, lattice structure, and whether Coulomb effects are included. This work is derived from and expands upon Ref. \cite{Sierk2022a}.

Our objective is to establish a systematic framework for computing excitation energies in small metallic clusters using tight-binding models. We begin by reviewing the formulation of TB models that account for light-matter interactions, presenting methods in both the velocity and length gauges. We examine the characteristics of these approaches in minimal cluster models, offering an exact analytical comparison of their excitation spectra. Subsequently, we apply these techniques to a four-atom Au cluster (Au$_4$) to investigate the influence of electron localization and crystal fields. Finally, we address practical considerations in constructing realistic TB models that go beyond simple regular-band extensions of Hubbard-model-like forms. Specifically, among the critical steps of generating such models, the symmetrization of excitonic Hamiltonians is analyzed in depth. This process must be performed exactly, respecting the irrep content of the single-particle excitations; otherwise, calculated excitations may exhibit incorrect symmetry. Since symmetry determines the decay channels of excitations, errors here can lead to fundamentally flawed conclusions. Therefore, we offer a complete guide to performing gauge-invariant symmetry analysis of Bloch functions using TB models, detailing how to determine symmetry in small clusters and how to exploit cluster symmetry during model construction. As an appendix to this general discussion, we consider the challenge of calculating excitation spectra in large clusters where the random-phase approximation (RPA) is employed to include screened Coulomb interactions. Finally, we outline future research directions. This manuscript is part of the author's doctoral

A notable example of this approach is the NONSTOP trial, which tests an intensive insulin regimen for hyperglycemia in the ICU for both ICU patients and outpatient surgical patients. Despite the intuitive expectation that intensive therapy would benefit all patients equally, a preliminary analysis revealed a potential interaction between patient type and treatment effect, leading to a post-hoc decision to analyze the intervention separately for each patient type. We propose a general method for determining when to conduct separate analyses in basket trials, applicable to any model parameterized by patient type. This approach involves comparing the data-driven estimate of a patient-type interaction parameter to a threshold derived from the patient-type random effect in a prior distribution. This method successfully identifies the need for separate analysis in the NONSTOP trial without requiring a post-hoc specification of the interaction parameter's scale. Furthermore, the approach is entirely data-driven, fully accounting for multiplicity when determining the threshold, and remains fully Bayesian in its analysis. The primary advantage of this methodology is that separate analyses for patient types are driven by the patient-type random effect, ensuring that patient types remain exchangeable and allowing for increased power in the experiment. Additionally, this approach is fully compatible with basket trial methodologies that evaluate patient types collectively. We illustrate the benefits of this methodology through a simulation study. Additionally, the R package BasketTrials, which facilitates the implementation of this approach, is publicly available. Our code is sufficiently general to be applied to a wide range of basket trial designs. Consequently, we encourage researchers to adopt separate analysis guidelines based on the patient-type interaction parameter when designing their own basket trials. This is particularly relevant when an interaction is plausible a priori, as in the NONSTOP trial, and when a clear pre-specified rule for when to conduct separate analyses is needed. We contend that this code-based approach is more appropriate than arbitrary sample-size thresholds for deciding on separate analyses. We also suggest that readers and reviewers of basket trial publications adopt separate analysis guidelines similar to those proposed in this paper. Relying on post-hoc sample-size arguments, as often seen in the literature, is not ideal when a patient-type interaction is plausible a priori. Such post-hoc sample-size thresholds can be interpreted as a form of p-hacking, potentially leading to incorrect decisions regarding when to perform separate analyses. By clearly specifying the criteria for separate analyses a priori, as this approach allows, one avoids the pitfalls inherent in post-hoc sample-size thresholds. This enables a more transparent, robust, and potentially more powerful trial analysis
