However, position-dependent dynamics in these systems significantly restrict the tracking performance achievable through traditional sequential loop closing (SLC) control strategies. This paper introduces a novel extension of the conventional SLC framework tailored for linear-parameter-varying systems, enabling the system to bypass limitations caused by position-dependent effects in high-precision applications. The benefits of this proposed control approach are validated through simulations using a high-fidelity model of a moving-magnet planar actuator, which displays position dependency in both actuation and sensing. Results demonstrate that the new control method surpasses conventional controls currently in deployment within industry settings. Furthermore, we establish performance criteria for next-generation motion systems. Significant findings from our analysis include: (a) the necessity for future motion systems to utilize measurement feedback to ensure high tracking accuracy; (b) the requirement for feedback sensors to maintain a high signal-to-noise ratio across all frequencies; (c) the imperative for lightweight system designs to exhibit constant stiffness across the operational trajectory; and (d) the need for future motion systems to integrate control design methodologies specifically optimized for high acceleration maneuvers. Finally, we outline performance targets for motion systems required to support terrestrial autonomous navigation across a broad spectrum of operational environments.

Terrestrial planar actuators are currently employed in applications spanning nanometer-scale positioning to movements exceeding one meter. Typical payloads range from grams to kilograms, operating across a wide spectrum of frequency bands—from sub-Hertz to hundreds of Hertz. Existing literature offers numerous motion control techniques designed for this payload and frequency spectrum. This review consolidates these various control strategies into a unified framework termed Sequential Loop Closing (SLC). We analyze the fundamental characteristics of systems governed by this protocol to derive key requirements for future control methodologies. Using these insights, we establish high-level performance objectives for next-generation motion systems. Additionally, we examine the distinct challenges associated with designing controllers for safety-critical systems. Our research yields several significant results regarding control design: (a) Future control techniques must be inherently robust, demonstrating a clear distinction between performance and safety: performance addresses how accurately a system executes its tasks, whereas safety concerns the stability of the feedback loop; (b) Position dependency significantly impedes tracking accuracy, implying that future controllers must be specifically optimized for position-dependent systems; and (c) It is essential to maintain a sufficient margin between the actuator's natural frequency and the system's primary resonant frequency. Building on these key points, we define the performance goals for motion systems

Since nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures correspond bijectively to real Killing spinors, the deformation framework can be expressed using spinors and Dirac operators. We demonstrate that the count of $p$-core $p'$-partitions corresponding to a fixed content $[\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_{p}]$ equals the number of standard Young tableaux with that content which avoid the permutation pattern $[p]$. Additionally, we provide an alternate bijection due to Baxter, connecting standard tableaux avoiding 123 with those avoiding 142, thereby relating the number of 3-core 5' partitions of content $[\mu_1,\mu_2]$ to the number of prime $q$ partitions with the same content. Bijections linking standard Young tableaux with specific content to those avoiding particular permutation patterns were initially discovered by Theodosiou, Psarros, and Baklavaris [17], who also noted a relation between 3-core 5' partitions and prime $q$ partitions. Our work extends these identities to broader sets of patterns and arbitrary numbers of cores. Specifically, we prove that for any content $[\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_{k}]$, the number of $p$-core $p'$-partitions avoiding a set of $s$ patterns is equal to the number of standard Young tableaux of $k$ rows with that content who also avoid those same $s$ patterns. To achieve this, vehicles employing a distributed architecture necessitate a distributed real-time scheduler (TR-S) equipped with fault management capabilities. Conventional distributed schedulers function by sending scheduled execution times to individual processors for independent local decisions, a method that fails to provide the required consistency and security guarantees. In this research, we propose a distributed schedule that is, in fact, a serial schedule. This approach enables the TR-S to manage faults on individual processors, ensuring a higher level of system reliability. We developed a mechanism for generating and maintaining this type of serial schedule in a real-time environment. Furthermore, we present a corresponding distributed scheduling algorithm. The design of this algorithm ensures that the system reaches a consistent state immediately following any processor failure, a critical requirement for distributed systems. Finally, we evaluated the computational complexity of our algorithm, a crucial factor for real-time systems, and demonstrated its effectiveness through simulation. Our complexity analysis confirmed that our approach guarantees both liveness and safety, with a time complexity of O(log n). This represents an improvement over the O(n) time complexity associated with standard distributed schedulers, a benefit derived from our use of a serial schedule. We achieved this without incurring additional space complexity, as our scheme does not require transmitting execution times to individual processors; instead, the TR-S retains all necessary data. Our approach is thus a novel contribution to the field of distributed scheduling. We demonstrated these results using a simulation tool, which we have made available for use by other researchers. This work has been published in the International Journal of Vehicle Chaos.

To address the bias-variance trade-off, various approaches have leveraged auxiliary information, with document modeling techniques notably enhancing the capacity to process text data. This capability allows for the extraction of textual insights related to users and items, facilitating the estimation of implicit feedback via an auxiliary model. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that REReMMT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with it achieving an average improvement of 12.06% over the second-best method on six real-world datasets. termed "local critic training," designed to address the challenges of distributed deep reinforcement learning (DLRL). While reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant practical success through the use of critic networks, current DLRL architectures often suffer from communication bottlenecks. Specifically, centralized critics require large batch sizes for effective policy gradients, causing agents to wait during value computation. Conversely, distributed critics, while allowing smaller batches, necessitate the exchange of statistics across all agents, creating delays during aggregation. These temporal disjoint opportunities for agent communication form the core inspiration for local critic training. The approach involves training local critic networks on individual agents with small batches between synchronization points and updating a central critic by aggregating their updates. Experiments demonstrate that local critic training enables smaller inter-interaction intervals while improving data freshness compared to existing distributed critic methods. Consequently, the proposed architecture scales better across increasing numbers of agents and supports larger problem sizes. We open-source our implementation as a PyTorch module within the Stable Baselines library at https://github.com/RobustnessSciences/lctraining. This code has also been utilized to generate experimental results for evaluating the method against current DLRL solutions.

Practical implications
 numerous algorithms rely on estimating entropy to calculate information-theoretic metrics such as mutual information. While Monte Carlo integration is a common method for this estimation, many relevant probability distributions are not easily expressible as closed-form formulas. This paper introduces an alternative technique for entropy estimation that is both highly accurate and comparable in computation time to standard methods such as Metropolis-Hastings. Furthermore, a specific implementation of this novel method is publicly available.

Questions addressed
 Numerous algorithms estimate entropy to determine other information-theoretic measures, such as mutual information. While general entropy estimation is typically handled via advanced Monte Carlo techniques like Metropolis-Hastings, can similar results be achieved using nested sampling? If so, does this approach offer any advantages?

Proposed solution
 Numerous algorithms estimate entropy to compute other information-theoretic measures, such as mutual information. Although general entropy estimation typically relies on Monte Carlo methods like Metropolis-Hastings, nested sampling can achieve comparable results. Is this possible? Yes, it is. Does this approach offer any advantages? Yes, it does.

Limitations
 nested sampling was not originally designed for entropy estimation, and our initial findings are not yet as accurate as those from other Monte Carlo techniques such as Metropolis-Hastings

Regarding the cardinal Stable Roommates with Inequalities problem, we establish that it is NP-complete under linear constraints but becomes solvable in polynomial time under quadratic ones. We also examine the cardinal Stable Marriage with Preferences and Questions problem, proving that checking the consistency of questions is NP-complete. However, we demonstrate that if questions are restricted to specific formats—such as comparing two agents or all four positions of a singleton tuple—resolution becomes possible in polynomial time. From an algorithmic perspective, although the general Stable Marriage with Questions problem is NP-complete, the restricted versions concerning questions about pairs and singletons can be solved in $O(n^3)$ time. By adapting the standard Gale-Shapley algorithm, we achieve a further improvement to $O(n^2)$. Last, although questions regarding couples can be inferred from questions about singles, our analysis shows that the general Stable Marriage with Preferences and Questions problem is parameterizedly NP-complete when parameterized by the number of questions an agent must answer.

Additionally, we show that for any $k \geq 2$, the weighted cardinally stable roommates problem is NP-complete with $k$ agents and $k$ distinct values in preference profiles. Although no polynomial-time algorithm exists for the general case, we present an $O(n^2p)$-time solution for four specific instances: triple questions, double questions, singleton questions, and zero-question scenarios. Additionally, for a fixed number of questions $h$, each instance can be solved in $O(n(\log n + \sigma))$ time, where $n$ represents the agent count, $\sigma$ denotes the total question count, and the solution relies on a binary search over sorted values combined with a linear-time stable matching algorithm for each resulting value partition.

However, the presence of volatile caches necessitates logging and explicitly flushing cache contents into NVM to guarantee consistency and correctness prior to a crash, a process that often incurs significant runtime overhead. This paper presents an algorithm-centric approach to establishing crash consistency for HPC applications within NVM environments. By simulating and analyzing one million realizations for various initial conditions—covering both equal and unequal mass configurations with random positions and velocities—we provide a complete benchmark for conditions under which existing statistical approximations are valid. These methods are widely utilized to model complex multi-wavelength variable sources, such as low-mass X-ray binaries and millisecond pulsars, whose light curves are influenced by both orbital variability and stochastic fluctuations in accumulated phase errors. Our results indicate that the standard "energy angular momentum statistical approximation" produces acceptable models for typical, randomly configured three-body systems but yields significant errors in non-hierarchical scenarios where it is otherwise applicable. Conversely, the simplified "random walk statistical approximation" is effective in certain highly hierarchical configurations but generates unrealistic models in most three-body dynamics regimes. Since random stochastic errors are inherently non-Gaussian, we introduce a new approach combining the random walk energy statistical approximation with a non-Gaussian probability distribution. Design mining applies machine learning methods to classify discussion artifacts, such as pull requests, as either related to design or not. This paper illustrates a basic example of design mining functionality, followed by an analysis showing that conclusion stability across different artifact types and repositories is unexpectedly low. We present an improved approach that leverages cross-repository information, demonstrating that this yields both higher performance and greater stability. Ultimately, we argue that a degree of artifact context is essential for effective design mining. Our discussion highlights potential applications and avenues for future research.

Miners are increasingly extracting data from Pull Requests (PRs), which include comments, associated issues, and linked code changes. Prior research has attempted to predict various attributes of PRs, such as author intent and success. However, these studies typically use independent data sources or simple artifact types like comments or issues. Conversely, application usage patterns suggest that gathering information from multiple linked artifacts creates a richer context for drawing conclusions. This paper introduces a methodology for analyzing PRs that integrates diverse data sources. We explore how this approach can predict four different attributes of a PR, revealing that it substantially surpasses state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that analyzing complete PRs is particularly significant for distinguishing between design-intent and non-design-intent authors. These findings suggest that leveraging multiple data sources is both highly feasible and significantly more effective for attribute prediction. Finally, we offer recommendations for future research in this field.

Pull request (PR) mining is a rapidly evolving field where researchers extract data from GitHub PR objects to automate the evaluation of a PR's purpose and achieve various goals. We synthesized 119 papers from 2016 to 2021 to create the first survey covering this emerging area. First, we categorized the methods into four artifact-level groups: pull request comments, associated issues, the PR itself, and the complete PR package. Second, we clustered these papers into seven research areas: purpose evaluation, refactoring, documentation, security, onboarding, and others. Across 19 subareas, we analyzed key findings and discussed how to replicate and extend current work. Looking ahead, we identify future research directions, including the need to move from design mining to design reasoning, the shift from design mining to design engineering, and the integration of design mining with design anthropology. Additionally, we emphasize the underexplored area of design mining across repositories and the challenge of incorporating human feedback

Notably, in numerous significant scenarios, the iteration count required to achieve a certain precision is independent of the problem's scale; consequently, the convergence of the proxi--tal method depends solely on this target precision rather than the number of variables. When applied to convex programming, these methods generate a sequence of problems with fewer variables that converge to a principal active subsystem. However, for general nonsmooth optimization, even first-order necessary conditions for optimality fail to guarantee a unique active subsystem, rendering proximal methods potentially nonconvergent. To address this, we introduce a principal value criterion for smoothness derived from Clarke's generalized gradient. We prove that if a convergent subsequence of a proximal method yields a limit point satisfying this criterion, it implies the existence of a unique principal active subsystem associated with that limit point. Furthermore, we present a numerical example involving equality constraints to demonstrate that the proposed criterion is essential for the convergence of proximal methods in nonsmooth contexts. Finally, we outline an improvement to the criterion that remains effective in the general case. By integrating this enhanced version, the principal value criterion becomes sufficient for optimality, enabling the application of proximal methods to solve convex programming problems based on this criterion. This approach facilitates the identification of a singular active subsystem for a given problem, even when the overall problem is not a convex programming task.

By employing a logarithmic carrier envelope offset (CEO) signal as the reference, this technique enables the precise measurement of atomic transition frequencies. Since the CEO is an continuous, dynamic signal, the method facilitates real-time, repetitive atomic frequency comparisons with high precision. In this work, we offer a unified theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of addressing these challenges. We establish core definitions, contrast architectural similarities and differences, and examine key training methodologies such as data modeling, augmenting specific relational inductive biases, and transfer learning. This study addresses these challenges by introducing a novel automatic mesh road crack detection system built on mesh road imagery captured from cameras mounted on maintenance vehicles. The proposed framework consists of four main stages: (1) preprocessing, (1a) Data Collection, (1b) Shadow Removal, (2) Augmentation, (3)Feature Extraction, and (4)Classification. The core algorithm utilizes Region 3D CNNs for crack classification. The integrated system demonstrates robust performance across diverse data sets collected from various vehicles under varying lighting conditions. Although trained solely on data set A, the system accurately identifies cracks in data set B with an overall accuracy of 95.68%, successfully distinguishing between cracked and non-cracked regions. Furthermore, the system effectively differentiates between cracks and both shadow and non-shadow areas, achieving 95.23% accuracy in classifying shadows against cracks. While other research has addressed similar challenges, this proposed system offers a more comprehensive approach by incorporating automatic data collection, extensive data augmentation techniques, and advanced deep learning classification methods. Key contributions of this research include: a) an automatic data collection mechanism leveraging computer vision and image stitching for wide-field of view imaging, b) advanced image augmentation strategies to enhance model generalizability, and c) a high-accuracy classification outcome achieved even when trained exclusively on data set A. Cracks are clearly detected in images from data set B, with accurate classification of cracked, no crack, and shadow regions.

While most existing algorithms assume that both the expert and the agent operate within the same Markov Decision Process (MDP), this paper investigates the more realistic scenario where the expert's domain may differ from the agent's. We introduce a method to learn a representation of the expert's MDP and integrate it into a counterfactual optimal transport regularized GAN for generating synthetic trajectories that approximate the expert's behavior. Extensive experiments are provided to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Code for our implementation can be found at https://github.com/MingdaShi2000/CounterfactualMT-GAN. In summary, this work offers a solution for imitation learning when the expert's MDP differs from that of the student, a scenario frequently encountered in practical applications such as driving and manufacturing. Our method utilizes a Counterfactual Optimal Transport GAN to extract a representation of the expert's policy or MDP and backpropagate counterfactual rewards through the GAN to update the agent's network, even in the absence of a shared state-space representation between the expert and the student. This enables the student to imitate the expert's policy without requiring a common state-space representation, a capability particularly relevant in domains like driving and manufacturing where expert-agent domain mismatches are common. By formulating imitation as a distributional matching problem between the student and the expert, we can counterfactually estimate the required distribution for the student to match the expert's behavior using a GAN. Our approach also incorporates a weighted adversarial loss derived from optimal transport theory, under the hypothesis that not all states contribute equally to successful task completion; states visited more frequently are assumed to be more significant for completing tasks. This enables the student to filter out noise from the expert's policy by assigning varying weights to different states during imitation. Code for our implementation is available at https://github.com/MingdaShi2000/CounterfactualMT-GAN. Keywords: Imitation Learning, Adversarial Networks, Counterfactual Matching. We address this by analyzing the mass spectrum of the Cygnus OB2 cluster using the MAJESTIC survey data. MAJESTIC offers a reliable distance of 2.4 kpc, utilizes a sensitive 0.87 MHz bandwidth line-of-sight survey tailored for sensitive absorption spectroscopy of pre-main-sequence stars, and ensures accurate proper motions and astrometry derived from ten-year Keck Adaptive Optics observations. Our investigation examines mass segregation within the young stellar population and employs a novel technique called "twin pairing," grounded in the assumption of isotropic fragment overabundance. This method relies on the concept of "twin pairs" formed when two fragments create a bound system while maintaining a constant mass ratio. The findings indicate that stars in Cygnus OB2 exhibit a consistent mass ratio of approximately 0.25 for these twins, confirming predictions from fragment overabundance theories and validating predictions from the Turbulent Clouds model. Furthermore, by constructing a synthetic model of the Cygnus OB2 initial mass function (IMF) based on the observed properties of its smallest fragments, we demonstrate that the majority of the cluster's mass is contained within the most massive star, thereby resolving the longstanding IMFMass problem.

However, existing methods often suffer from either excessive computational cost or a limited search space. This paper introduces a novel, concise, and efficient fraction-based association rule miner. For applications where the search space is restricted, we also propose a tailored algorithm to rapidly enumerate rules. Our main method not only accelerates the discovery of rules within the vast search space but also functions effectively for applications involving small numbers of items and conditions. Drawing on North Carolina court data from 1994 to 2009, this study assesses whether mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation reduces the probability of future re-offending. Their primary value lies in the ability to predict interference levels and channel gains at unexplored spatial locations. While current radio map estimation techniques depend on sensor data from fixed or uncontrollable positions, this paper introduces a novel approach where a UAV actively gathers measurements along a specific flight path. This trajectory is optimized to generate precise radio map estimates within a minimal timeframe. The underlying route planning strategy employs a map uncertainty metric to prioritize data collection at locations offering the highest informational value. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed strategy significantly outperforms standard methods, such as uniform flight paths and maps derived from sparse or unrelated data, achieving up to a 20% increase in map estimation accuracy. Ultimately, this efficient and intelligent approach facilitates enhanced and more accurate sensing, which is crucial for optimizing network decisions like base station placement and UAV trajectory design. Furthermore, the method can be easily adapted for real-world applications. The approach assigns a K-L divergence score to each test observation; significantly higher scores indicate anomalies. We establish that, under a parabolic model for the K-L divergence between the true data distribution and the generator, the score for an outlier converges in distribution to a value strictly exceeding the true distribution's score as the sample size grows. Furthermore, using a large deviation principle, we extend this convergence result from scores of single observations to the maximum score across the test data. Leveraging these theoretical findings, we demonstrate that the method achieves consistent detection: with sufficient data, the method can identify the presence of an anomaly in new, unseen data with a score exceeding a predefined threshold. Our approach requires no modeling of the test data's distribution and only assumes that the K-L divergence between the true generator and true test data distributions is bounded. Additionally, we propose a simple method for estimating the K-L divergence between true data and generator distributions via empirical scores. Finally, both the consistency and efficacy of the proposed approach are validated through numerical experiments.

Existing approaches rely entirely on modality-specific validation; however, this study proposes a framework to assess a model's robustness by examining modality-specific validation mechanisms. Multi-modal learning seeks to leverage features from sequential data to enhance predictions in tasks such as video object recognition. However, the efficacy of these models depends entirely on the quality of hand-crafted visual and auditory features. This work introduces a novel, fully-supervised, end-to-end audio-visual object recognition model that automatically extracts auditory features from a single recording. The proposed approach leverages sequential spatial information across multiple video frames to generate a richer audio representation for audio-visual object recognition. Experiments were conducted using two datasets: Action Recognition 2013 and CUAD. Notably, the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art supervised audio-visual object recognition techniques. Additionally, empirical results demonstrate that incorporating sequential spatial information yields superior auditory representations for bi-modal object recognition. The source code is available at https://github.com/aidasakoulis/CSVOR.

In standard supervised object detection and segmentation, multiple instances of the same class are typically averaged. We hypothesize that the sequential spatial arrangement of these instances within an image or video holds valuable information for subsequent tasks, such as scene or activity recognition. To validate this, we conducted experiments using frames extracted from videos. Our approach demonstrates how spatial configurations of objects, including their counts, can be effectively aggregated into ordered sequences and utilized for both audio-visual object recognition and scene description. Results indicate that this method outperforms fully-supervised visual scene description approaches. Recently, the One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) framework was proposed to broaden the scope of traditional differential privacy methods by enhancing data utility, leveraging the insight that not every record carries sensitive information. However, prior research operated under the assumption that all records were statistically independent. Driven by the context of occupancy data within building management systems, we broaden the OSDP framework. Our contribution rests on two key insights: first, OSDP can better leverage structure in occupancy data by generating synthetic data reflecting local dependencies; second, records within a dataset may exhibit independence structure that is known in advance, allowing for wider OSDP privacy regions. We validate the practicality of our approach through experiments on synthetic occupancy datasets featuring various types of known local dependency structures. Our evaluation demonstrates that our method achieves superior privacy utility by producing more informative synthetic data while simultaneously enabling provable one-sided privacy guarantees. This study systematically investigates the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of emission knots in gas density substructures using spatially resolved spectra, departing from previous analyses that relied solely on spatial data. Utilizing hydrodynamical simulations of a Keplerian disk governed by viscous contraction, we apply radiative transfer techniques to model emission spectra, thereby linking gas dynamics to observable spectral characteristics. This study extends the findings of Cannarsa and Capuani to the specific context of mean field games of controls. In this framework, controls represent velocities; however, ensuring equilibrium existence poses significant challenges when requiring in-place invariance, a task that is typically more complex than it appears. We address these difficulties by leveraging the theory of geodesic variations in optimal transport. This mathematical framework enables the characterization of optimal transport plans as couplings between probability measures on the configuration space, which corresponds to the product of one-dimensional mean field game solutions. Following the approach of Capuani, we demonstrate that the product of two existence results yields an existence result for the original problem. Furthermore, as noted in the literature, the solution to the one-dimensional mean field game of controls can be interpreted as a weak solution to a first-order partial differential equation. The product of two such weak solutions remains a weak solution to a system of two first-order PDEs, a property that facilitates the derivation of formal a priori estimates. These estimates are sufficiently robust to support Capuani's approximation argument for the solution. Finally, Capuani's approximation is readily applicable in our setting due to the specific structure of our problem, as it relies on parameters rather than the full solution. This allows for the straightforward construction of a sequence of smooth solutions that converges to the regular solution identified by Capuani.

Central to this domain is the Second Law, formulated as a monotone under free transformations that establishes an order on physical states. Furthermore, the "resource strength" derived from optimal extraction yields—known as resource measures—offers a quantitative definition of states within these processes. In general resource processes, we characterize a second-law measure as the infimum of a specific type of value obtained by applying a free measurement to a quantum system in a given state. Any monotone that is co-continuous decomposable can be expressed as a weighted sum of these second-law measures, a result that provides an optimal decomposition into quantum one-resource states. Extending this, we introduce a broader class of resources, termed bi-potent quantum one-resource states, which are significantly simpler than arbitrary quantum states. Uniquely, any quantum state can be represented as a convex combination of these bi-potent resources; notably, these resources are not themselves bi-potent. Finally, we explore the interplay between bi-potent resources and monotones, revealing a partial order of monotones that parallels the order of resources in free transformations, along with an characterization of the minimal elements in this framework. as a macroscopic model for investigating material failure. This system simulates a two-dimensional particle framework subjected to uniaxial strain, allowing for the analysis of how strain and strain-rate affect failure characteristics. Experiments were conducted using plastic珠s of varying diameters (0.897 cm, 0.495 cm, and 0.295 cm) on a clean water surface within a rectangular tank 20 cm wide and 100–150 cm long. The expansion was driven by an motorized belt running along the tank's rear edge. High-speed recordings at 200 frames per second tracked both horizontal and vertical positions. To ensure the motion remained affine and strain was uniform across the sample, particle density was maintained low, typically around 0.02 particles per square centimeter. For each particle type, approximately 20 independent failure events were captured. Additionally, numerical simulations were performed on arrays of particles connected by harmonic springs to correlate macroscopic observations with microscale interaction forces.

Failure in the particle rafts consistently followed a localized mode. Depending on the specific parameters, the failure structure manifested as either a single diagonal band or a series of sequential blocks resembling those seen in sandpile failures. From the failure structures recorded in high-speed videos, microscopic yield forces between particles and the evolution of average interparticle spacing were quantitatively derived. When normalized by the average interparticle distance at the onset of failure, the average microscopic yield force diminished slightly just prior to failure across all parameters. Furthermore, the ratio of the magnitude of this average yield force to the magnitude of fluctuating yield forces remained relatively constant and independent of particle size, provided the system was sufficiently close to the failure state.

Across all parameters, the time-averaged velocity of the liquid surface remained constant throughout the expansion. However, the time-averaged velocity difference between the top and bottom surfaces increased linearly with applied macroscopic strain at a rate dependent on the parameter set. Consequently, the ratio of top-to-bottom velocity at any point remained approximately constant and did not change significantly as parameters varied, provided the system was near failure. This allowed the use of a single timescale to characterize all parameters, termed "effective macroscopic strain." Using this metric, all parameters converged to a single value for the ratio of the magnitude of the microscopic average yield force to the magnitude of the top velocity at the system's center.

However, this domain remains underexplored, with existing studies yielding only marginal gains in embedding quality and utility. A primary driver of this limitation is the incomplete modeling of time within current time-aware KGE frameworks. This paper introduces a novel approach to simultaneously knowledge and time embedding through the concept of "time slices." Rather than distributing a time range uniformly as previous methods do, we concentrate on specific moments, such as around time $t$. To facilitate this, we represent time not as a single point but as an interval focused on $t$, defined by before-$t$ and after-$t$ boundaries that are asymmetric and unevenly spaced as one approaches $t$. This approach offers two key advantages: (a) it enables the capture of more granular and localized time semantics for time-sensitive knowledge, and (b) it accommodates varying granularities for different datasets or knowledge subsets. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm that our method significantly improves both embedding quality and performance on time-aware link prediction, substantially surpassing all prior state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, our results demonstrate a substantial reduction in parameter count compared to previous approaches, even under the most stringent granularities. Finally, we present qualitative analyses of the generated embeddings to elucidate the superior learning of time semantics achieved by our model. Our code will be made available on GitHub.

Since pre-trained Language Models (LMs) cannot store all necessary information, they are frequently augmented by retrieving relevant data from external sources to form local representations for reading comprehension. This study focuses on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and introduces the generation-guided generation (GiG) approach, where the generation process consists of two stages: guided retrieval followed by generation. MiDaFS is employed as a representative RAG technique to execute guided retrieval. MiDaFS uses the current token as a query to retrieve the most pertinent context from the source, which then serves as expanded input for the language model. This multi-stage framework is anticipated to mitigate issues in one-stage RAG methods, thereby enhancing the local representation of current tokens and improving generation performance. To validate this hypothesis, GiG is applied to represent the simplified two-stage RAG setup in MiDaFS. Experimental results demonstrate that GiG significantly improves performance over one-stage RAG in both closed- and open-domain settings. Qualitative analysis further reveals that guided retrieval effectively retrieves more semantically relevant information about entities, thereby enriching the input for generation and enabling better performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/opendomainqa/GiG. This work aims to promote the development of retrieval-augmented NLP models.

Our construction begins with a class of complexes—expander simulators for homology. Despite this, we conjecture that simulators for homology represent an inherently harder combinatorial problem, analogous to the distinction between random walks and uniform sampling. While measurements using multi-channel magnetic antennas are a viable solution, locating optimal spots for sensing multiple frequencies simultaneously within crowded environments remains difficult. A more promising approach involves scanning a single MW magnetic sensor across a small area to capture a spatial spectrum of signals. This method enables the determination of whether the scanned region contains a specific target object and allows for the simultaneous detection of objects in proximity. By integrating data from a spatial spectrum acquired via MW magnetic sensing, this technique offers robust solutions for scanning objects in hidden zones inaccessible to camera-based sensing or optical imaging. Our proposed method demonstrates high precision in detecting targeted objects by effectively mitigating interference and multipath effects. Additionally, we introduced a novel signal separation technique tailored for MW magnetic sensing, capable of isolating up to four distinct objects operating at different frequencies within a small area. This approach significantly expands the potential applications of MW magnetic sensing, particularly for hidden targets where conventional methods fall short, and further accelerates its adoption in areas such as navigation, localization, and security. Our findings suggest that this proposed method can distinguish targets based on their location within a small scanned area with sub-centimeter accuracy, even amidst complex interference conditions. Despite their utility, their deep recurrent connections often render them prone to training instability caused by gradient vanishing or explosion during backpropagation through time (BPTT). Although strategies like gradient clipping, network normalization, careful weight initialization, and architecture selection have been devised to address these issues, there remains a lack of comprehensive empirical comparisons among these methods, leaving creators uncertain about the optimal stability enhancements for their specific contexts. In this study, we systematically evaluate various gradient stability techniques, focusing on their individual and combined effects on performance, particularly regarding random seeds, initialization schemes, and time-series datasets. Our experiments utilize grids of network hyper-parameters to locate the best configurations for each setup. We demonstrate that while the proposed methods significantly broaden the range of stable recurrent networks, combining normalization with appropriate weight initialization yields superior results, offering both conceptual insights and practical guidance for practitioners. Notably, this approach enhances the generalization capacity of existing architectures; for instance, normalization paired with LeakyReLU activation functions substantially improves the generalization of LSTMs, even outperforming shallow networks like MLPs in certain time-series forecasting tasks. Overall, these findings offer robust solutions for greatly stabilizing recurrent networks, including LSTMs, to effectively predict time-series data, regardless of duration, through automated hyperparameter tuning. This work underscores the pivotal role of normalization in unlocking the full potential of recurrent networks. For practical applications, we provide pre-trained models featuring the recommended hyperparameters for multiple tasks using standard architectures. This capability highlights the presence of a universal recurrent unit capable of generalizing across tasks, thereby offering strong evidence against the need for an internal clock in these architectures. These discoveries offer deep insights into the capabilities of recurrent networks, facilitating their efficient deployment with high performance. All experiments were conducted using TensorFlow 2.x on over 100,000 distinct tasks to derive reliable statistical conclusions. While deep learning has driven significant breakthroughs, it remains a data hungry approach. Efficient Knowledge Integration (EKI) facilitates the incorporation of structured knowledge to enhance learning efficiency, reduce dependency on data, and improve robustness. This survey focuses on deep learning models that integrate two primary knowledge types: world knowledge, which includes logical constraints and reasoning rules, and parameter knowledge, encompassing transfer and meta-learning parameters. We categorize these methods into two groups: integrating parameter knowledge and integrating logical knowledge. Additionally, we highlight that EKI is vital for machine learning optimization, meta-learning, reasoning, and knowledge graph embedding. The repository is available at https://github.com/yhli1208/Machine-Learning-With-Knowledge-Graphs, which will be updated continuously.

Connecting structured knowledge to machine learning models boosts performance, improves generalization, and increases data efficiency. This work reviews deep learning approaches that integrate two key knowledge types: logical knowledge, such as semantic relationships and reasoning rules, and parameter knowledge, such as meta-learning parameters and transfer learning weights. The survey covers three main areas: Embedding Logical Knowledge, Learning with Parameter Knowledge, and Reasoning with Knowledge Graphs. We also discuss the evaluation of both logical and parameter knowledge. While extensive, the field evolves daily, so we invite submissions of missing papers or duplicate sections via pull requests. while high-order interactions in large graphs encode valuable real-world dynamics, extracting these higher-order structures from original transactions is labor-intensive due to the noisy and irregular nature of sources. Consequently, most existing methods focus on utilizing pre-existing, well-defined graphs to uncover higher-order patterns. Furthermore, the disjoint and scattered PN-junctions in typical extraction processes hinder the analysis of massive graphs, as most state-of-the-art algorithms struggle with both higher-order interactions and scale. To overcome these limitations, we introduce HO-HQS (Higher Order Homophily Quotient Structure), a novel approach for discovering high-order structure functions in large-scale graph data. Specifically, we employ higher-order hyperedges to represent local interactions within graphs, defined by hyperedges with low in-degree (connected to few output nodes) and high out-degree (connected to many output nodes). Additionally, we develop an efficient algorithm to compute HO-HQS for large graphs, demonstrating through theoretical analysis and experiments on both synthetic and real datasets that this method is not only fast but also effective in revealing crucial data structure dynamics pre-existing in large graphs. Finally, to the best of our knowledge, this work marks the first step toward faster and more effective application of higher-order interaction discovery in large graph data. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/zhangyq18/HO-HQS.

We extend weak noise theory, which translates large deviations into a non-linear hydrodynamic framework, by demonstrating its full solvability via a link to the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Our findings complement and extend previous work [1, 2斥], addressing the gap regarding space-dependent fluctuations above the KPZ roughness in higher dimensions. Although large deviations specifically demand more regularity than standard fluctuations, they share similar scale dependencies governed by the renormalization group. Specifically, the leading term of the large deviations action for a space-dependent fluctuation $\phi(x)$ remains independent of the kinetic coefficient $\nu$, whereas it scales with the surface tension $\sigma$ according to the relation $\nu^{|\!1-3/|\!1+2}}$. Gerrymandering refers to the distortion of elections through the manipulation of district boundaries; however, verifying this requires considerable analytical effort. This work aims to generalize a simulation environment capable of inferring unfair practices in districts via Bayesian inference. Our approach involves adapting a redistricting Markov Chain Monte Carlo method, enhanced with Simulated Annealing, to rapidly produce representative voting distributions and clearly expose unfair biases affecting voter populations. This technique not serves as a robust environment for generating representative elections but also illustrates how Simulated Annealing can generalize across various states and districts. Furthermore, we demonstrate its suitability as a sampling method for applying artificial intelligence. Additionally, we summarize the historical development of adapters created to infer unfairness in redistricting.

We introduce TextUnifiedGameEngine (TEXTUGEN), a unified, modular, and extensible Python framework designed to streamline the development of text games for evaluating agent agents. TEXTUGEN streamlines experiment construction by offering high-level methods for parsing test cases, evaluating agents, and gathering data. Its modules cover essential functionalities including language understanding, task planning, self-modeling, data collection, and analysis. To demonstrate TEXTUGEN's utility, we included three existing games from the existing literature, which have been adapted into corresponding modules. Our inclusion criteria for these examples were: (1) prior evaluation of agent agents, (2) open-source implementation, and (3) implementation via text-based games. Users can readily reproduce and extend TEXTUGEN using the examples and sources provided in our repository. Additionally, TEXTUGEN significantly accelerates future research by enabling the quick creation of new game modules. Qualitatively, TEXTUGEN is anticipated to be valuable for open research in areas such as life games, programming game extensions, and collaborative virtual agent tasks. Quantitatively, TEXTUGEN has already saved researchers approximately one to two months per experiment since its release in mid-2021, which will continue to reduce time as the library matures. Given that TEXTUGEN was developed from established papers and implementations, it accurately reflects current research practices and effectively extends their contributions. We invite contributions from the community to generate new game modules, research papers, and application papers to further enrich the library. Anisotropy, a common property in various plasmas, arises from non-isotropic energy sources, such as lasers interacting with plasma, which generally bias electron motion in a specific direction. This modifies the dielectric properties used in general plasma wave propagation analyses, making it more complex. Under these scenarios, experiments have confirmed that plasmas exhibit a directional dependence in their permittivity, known as anisotropic permittivity. This concept has been utilized to develop anisotropic plasma lenses capable of focusing or defocusing electron beams, with deflection angles matching isotropic results. Additionally, under appropriate conditions, anisotropic plasma slabs can produce extraordinary and ordinary images, similar to optical crystals. This is attributed to the different reflection and refraction behaviors of ordinary and extraordinary plasmons when entering or exiting the plasma. This image formation phenomenon can be interpreted using general relativity principles. This work presents a general analysis of the material properties of anisotropic media, including isotropic, conjugate, and hyperbolic types, under finite potential conditions. It explores how the direction of particle motion relative to the anisotropy source affects the plasma's dielectric behavior, preparing the ground for a comprehensive analysis of plasmoid formation in atomic-scale anisotropic plasmas. The study highlights that the dielectric characteristics of an anisotropic plasma region can be represented as a generally anisotropic curved spacetime metric. This approach provides a method to calculate the transmission coefficient through a finite, anisotropic plasma region using general relativity transformations applied to general waves. The resulting formula aligns with the one derived in plasma physics literature, confirming its validity under appropriate conditions. By comparing outcomes from two distinct approaches, we establish a general framework for investigating potential applications of anisotropic plasmas within the context of transformed optics. This study examines individual-level data from 1,117 Swedish seniors (aged 77+) to analyze the impacts of COVID-19 and vaccination on their activities and interactions. The findings indicate that vaccinated individuals experienced fewer infections, fewer hospitalizations, and heightened fear. Furthermore, those with lower pre-vaccination activity levels saw an increase in their engagements post-vaccination, suggesting that health anxiety drove senior citizens to become more active and social following immunization. Our findings are dimension-independent, and the requirements imposed on the driving noises are minimal. These results rely fundamentally on criteria previously developed by the authors and T. As an application, we derive the ergodicity of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, noting that our result encompasses the weakly dissipative case involving pure jump degenerate noise. Furthermore, our criterion requires less regularity from the driving noises compared to existing criteria used to prove ergodicity in similar systems. In addition to direct estimation techniques, we utilize a novel approximation via resolvent equations for solutions to stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations. Finally, we compare our results with those obtained for stochastic Navier-Stokes equations and stochastic heat equations. Furthermore, examples of sufficient conditions for ergodicity are provided, including those involving multiple compounding noises. Notably, determining specific forms of compounding noises that yield ergodicity represents a challenging issue. However, our criteria indicate that ergodicity can be achieved even when driven by simple compounding noises, such as Poisson or Casimir processes. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $\delta$-variation condition on coefficients is a necessary condition for ergodicity in stochastic heat equations. Regarding stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, the $\delta$-variation condition is necessary only in the scenario where all imaginary parts vanish or are non-zero. Emphasizing the significance of decoupling techniques, we utilize them to prove irreducibility and establish the novel approximation result mentioned earlier. This work extends the approach in [37] regarding ergodicity in stochastic heat equations. Finally, we illustrate how decoupling methods can be employed to estimate solutions boundedly in $L_p$-Bogoliubov spaces, thereby proving the ergodicity of real-valued stochastic heat equations. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operating on sparse matrices by leveraging the structural properties of these matrices. Our observations reveal that the performance gains from applying standard optimization techniques, such as memoization and caching, are largely attributable to the sparsity-induced similarity among node features at different layers. Generally, the degree of similarity among node features increases as we move to higher layers, while the matrix sparsity decreases; however, the overall computational efficiency remains dependent on the matrix's sparsity pattern. We evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed approach across various GNN architectures, including GCN, GAT, GPNet, and SAGE, confirming its broad applicability. The results indicate that significant performance improvements can be achieved with a modest reduction in model accuracy. Experimental data shows that applying these optimizations to a 5-layer GNN model reduces the average computation time per sample by approximately 40%, with even greater gains possible when node features contain more dimensions. Furthermore, we introduced a refined method capable of further accelerating training. This Refined Adaptive Method dynamically selects the super-subset of nodes to memoize or cache during each batch, adapting the process to the specific characteristics of the data rather than applying uniform transformations to all nodes. Additionally, a novel, efficient algorithm for calculating the k-core of a graph was utilized to identify well-connected nodes within the training set. These features vary computationally based on their clustering, allowing for the customization of computation strategies to their specific nature. The proposed methods are broadly applicable to any training data, as they rely exclusively on the graph structure and do not require knowledge of the target labels, unlike most data-dependent methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/di4k/4COGNN. Our findings demonstrate that the average computational efficiency can be improved by approximately a factor of 2.5. Given the empirical validation across diverse scenarios, these methods are both generally and specifically applicable to a wide range of graphs and tasks. Consequently, this research opens up new directions for structural computation optimizations within graph-based machine learning. Keywords: Graph Neural Networks, Memoization, Caching, k-core, Efficiency.

Unlike traditional Trojan attacks that embed small, insignificant patterns onto clean host images, our approach treats triggers as complete images representing semantically relevant object classes. Because the backdoored classifier learns the abstract semantics of these trigger images instead of specific pixel patterns, it can be activated by visually distinct yet semantically similar inputs. ### Requirements

The system must satisfy three primary requirements regarding data handling and processing:

1. **Support various formats:** Accommodate multiple data types and structures to ensure compatibility with both existing pipelines and a broad spectrum of output formats.
2. **Reduce data sizes:** Minimize data volume during both in-box processing and final writing to optimize storage efficiency.
3. **Rapid write to diverse storage mediums:** Execute fast data writes to various storage types to maximize the utilization of all available bandwidth.

Complementary high-precision ground-based spectroscopy combined with the direct imaging of exoplanets offers a promising pathway to determine the bulk compositions and internal structures of these bodies. This work employs Bayesian Bayesian analysis to create a dynamical forward model that calculates the relationship between Earth-analogue internal structures—specifically internal composition, rotation rate, magnetic field strength, and orbital semi-major axis—and observable quantities including boundary pressures, boundary radii, heat flux, heat generation, surface temperature, bulk composition, surface chemistry, spectral features, collisional erosion, photometric data, and collision impactor properties. A third example demonstrates Bayesian analysis linking the internal structure of an Earth-analogue planet to various observational data points and uncertainties, supported by related inference methods and best practices for Bayesian modeling of such systems. Finally, we leverage this approach to provide an abstract characterization of Topological Spaces via the 2-functor of modal languages to Topological Categories over Set. This characterization utilizes solely the semantics of modal language relative to set-based topological categories, thereby resolving a longstanding question about a purely semantic characterization of Topological Spaces. Our proof relies on renowned concepts from functorial semantics in categorical logic and reveals, for the first time, a deep and previously unrecognized connection between topological categories and modal logic. Furthermore, our method allows for the modular construction of numerous topological categories over Set from a single "basic" topological category over Set by leveraging the 2-functoriality of the modal language. This paves the way for conceptualizing the modular architecture of modal logic and its extensive historical development. The trivial topological category over Set, featuring a single map from a singleton to empty set and a universal pullback functor, is shown to contain all fundamental ingredients for a rich theory of topological categories over Set. These include the notions of pullbacks, product spaces, constant functors, limit functors, free languages, and the universally valid sentences of the language. We believe that (and hopefully) this establishes a novel, robust, and elegant foundation for modal logic. This work aims to contribute to numerous ongoing research questions within the methodology of modal logic and topological categories over Set, particularly within the emerging discipline of topological semantics for modal logic. Finally, we provide significant support for rejecting the methodology of topological functors over Set for modal logic, although a fully rigorous demonstration requires advanced research beyond the scope of this paper. As a rule of thumb, the modal logic characterized by a topological category over Set can be interpreted as a sub-logic of the logic characterized by the corresponding topological functor over Set.

usion model initially introduced by Fisher to describe allele spread in genetic populations and later generalized by Kolmogorov for broader contexts, is addressed using a new technique for solving nonlinear partial differential equations. This method yields a unique approximate solution that defies intuition. While the solution adheres to the maximum principle, its time-dependent behavior collapses for all positive times, rendering it highly irregular and non-smooth; consequently, the frequently used traveling wave approximation is invalidated. In contrast to traditional duration modeling techniques that rely on specific distributional assumptions (such as Gaussian) and utilize the mean for synthesis, our approach can theoretically represent any distribution defined over non-negative integers. When applied phone-wise, the model offers several benefits: it leverages the full context available in acoustic models, enables the approximation of any duration distribution including modal values, and maintains a single model for all speakers and accents rather than relying on separate duration and acoustic models. Despite being trained on discrete labels, the model supports differentiable training via a categorical distribution matched with pointwise mutual information regularization. Frame-wise generation is sampled via a greedy strategy, subsequently rounded to the nearest integer. Phone-level generation is achieved through beam search. Evaluations conducted on TIMIT, Librivox, and the Japanese News Corpus demonstrate that the method achieves estimation accuracy comparable to conventional approaches and yields promising results for forced alignment. Furthermore, speech synthesis performed with this approach sounds natural when compared to Gaussian duration models. Both forced alignment and synthesis metrics indicate that the model provides a more precise estimate of the duration mode compared to point estimation methods. However, the model occasionally generates excessive pauses, an issue that can be mitigated using unlabeled data for speaker-specific refinement. This study introduces an extended occupancy model that allows data points—specifically fishing sets—in small-scale fisheries to capture the spatial aggregation of target fish. The model's parameters are estimated using a Bayesian framework, with posterior parameter distributions applied to infer aggregation intensity for various fish species. Using data from coastal fishing communities in Honduras, we first validated the model against real-world fish aggregation theory. Subsequently, we compared the results of this new modelized dataset with those from a conventional occupancy model. Finally, we utilized the modelized parameters to generate future forecasts for target catch species, revealing that the traditional occupancy model failed to do so effectively. Our findings confirm that the model successfully estimates fish aggregation levels, aligning with established ecological principles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that accounting for spatial aggregation is essential, as a traditional occupancy model can bias species presence estimates by up to 50%. Additionally, the model proves superior to its traditional counterpart for forecasting, a benefit that becomes increasingly significant as environmental changes and climate change exacerbate uncertainty. Although developed for colonial fish species, this approach is adaptable for applying occupancy modeling to other aggregated organisms across various fields. Ultimately, we propose this model as a novel method to enhance the forecasting capabilities of single-community time-series, a critical tool for community-based fisheries. This is achieved without the need for multi-temporal data or increased fieldwork efforts, thereby maintaining support for local sustainability and conservation strategies. This approach represents an advancement over the current state-of-the-art, which has thus far been limited to applications on non-aggregated species.

This process begins with a skin lesion capture, followed by communication between the patient and telemedicine specialist. the correctness of multi-threaded programs, surpassing the limitations of unit and functional tests which often fail to detect race conditions. McMin involves constructing a graph grammar that models all possible thread interleavings, where production applications represent specific events; during grammar derivation, the program's dynamic invariant is maintained. Detour model checking detours around certain productions to explore deeper thread interleavings. Although effective, both approaches suffer from exponential complexity due to the potential for an exponential number of intermediate grammars relative to program size, necessitating optimizations to ensure practical usability. This paper evaluates various detour techniques for minimal detour model checking on multi-threaded programs. Results demonstrate that specific configurations of the detour grammar can avoid generating intermediate grammars, reducing complexity from exponential to a lower-order polynomial (based on program size and grammar size), while broader configurations yield only polynomial complexity without sacrificing exploration power. Detour model checking detours around certain productions to explore deeper thread interleavings.

Minimal detour model checking serves as a formal technique for detecting race conditions in multi-threaded programs by constructing a graph grammar that models all potential thread interleavings. An extension, the open minimal detour graph grammar, was proposed to explore equivalent derivations in parallel, reducing worst-case complexity from exponential to quadratic by limiting the number of intermediate grammars. Model checking operations are mapped to a graph grammar, with intermediate grammars filtered to retain only those satisfying program-invariant subgraphs. However, this approach still incurs quadratic complexity, as filtering requires copying the entire grammar after each open-minimal detour application.

Meanwhile, partition-based open minimal detour graph grammars were introduced to explore deeper interleavings by allowing multiple copies of a node to exist simultaneously within the graph. Detours are restricted to opening edges between specific partition classes, rather than all specified edges. While this reduces the upper-bound complexity to a lower-order triangular polynomial, intermediate grammars must still be copied following each model check operation.

Further generalizing this method, partition-based open minimal partition graph grammars allow for probing specific partition configurations to check for race conditions. Detours are prohibited between certain partition classes to delve into deeper interleavings. Exploration is modeled as a graph grammar where each node represents a partition of graph elements. Multiple nodes can exist within a single grammar to represent various partition configurations, but no intermediate grammars are ever copied. Since the number of partitions is bounded by the program's thread count, complexity remains triangular. Race conditions are detected when two or more non-synchronized partitions contain conflicting labels.

One such problem involves the discrepancy between the electroweak scale ($v\sim 246$ GeV) and the Planck scale ($M_{\rm{P}}\sim 1.229\times 10^{2}$ GeV). Another pertains to the Higgs mass ($m_h\sim 125$ GeV) compared to the reduced Planck mass ($M_{\rm{p}}\equiv M_{\rm{P}}/\sqrt{8\pi}\sim 2$ TeV). To investigate these issues within supergravity, we focus on the $F$- and $D$-term mechanisms regarding the Higgs mass hierarchy problem. We demonstrate how to derive effective supergravity models from supersymmetric string theory, specifically heterotic string theory, by integrating string theory constraints into supergravity Lagrangians. Within this context, we construct a SUSY $SO(10)$ gauge group model with extra fields using a string action, specifically the non-supersymmetric type IIB string action, as a concrete example of string action. By applying an orbifold projection followed by breaking the $SO(10)$ gauge group to a $SU(5)$ gauge group using Chan-Paton factors, we obtain an effective type $0\rm{b}$ supergravity model featuring the $SU(5)$ gauge group. This resulting supergravity model incorporates various scalar multiplets capable of facilitating $F$- and $D$-term solutions to the Higgs mass hierarchy problem, along with scalar leptons and quarks suitable for quantum gravity corrections to the Standard Model. Finally, we calculate the quantum correction coefficients for the Higgs mass in this effective supergravity model using the renormalization group equation. Our findings indicate that the proposed model can successfully resolve the Higgs mass hierarchy problem. One possible reason for the success of this supergravity model in addressing the Higgs mass hierarchy problem is its derivation from the heterotic string theory lagrangian, which is coupled to $N=1$ supergravity. Additionally, we show that our supergravity model can be directly extended to an $F$- and $D$-term solution for the strong coupling constant hierarchy problem. In this study, we introduce a novel form of nonreciprocity that manifests in photon pair correlations rather than linear transmission. We provide both experimental and theoretical validation of this effect within the second-order coherence functions of photon pairs generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Crucially, reversing the pump propagation direction can cause significant extinction of these coherence functions while leaving the pump transmission unchanged. Our findings establish that nonreciprocity is not merely a property of linear transmission but also extends to nonlinear phenomena. Consequently, this insight opens up new avenues for the development and application of nonreciprocal devices that operate via nonlinear mechanisms. Furthermore, our work sheds light on the broader context of directional dependence in nonlinear processes and their interaction with radiation. Specifically, we demonstrate that a substantial contribution of evanescent fields to the pump's electromagnetic field can be leveraged to realize strong nonreciprocity in transmission-independent nonlinear responses. This establishes photon pair correlations as a potential tool for probing the electromagnetic properties of highly integrated optical systems. Ultimately, our results indicate that achieving nonreciprocity without relying on material nonlinearity is feasible only when the product of linear coupling and material gain is balanced against the pump wavelength's group velocity. Given that our nonlinear mechanism is independent of group velocity, it is possible to obtain a large nonlinear response even when the pump group velocity is near zero, thereby enabling the realization of a nonlinear nonreciprocity close to perfect extinction. Consequently, our results facilitate the attainment of large nonlinear nonreciprocity approximately two orders of magnitude beyond what is achievable through standard linear magnetic isolation methods. This establishes nonlinear nonreciprocity as a foundational concept for optically isolating components in high-index nonlinear circuits where magnetic isolation is ineffective. Finally, we show that nonlinear nonreciprocity reaches perfect extinction when either the pump or the signal/idler modes are at their critical coupling points. This insight offers a fresh perspective on the design of isolated nonlinear optical components, particularly in scenarios where only one of the pump, signal, or idler modes satisfies the critical coupling condition. Our work thus enables the creation of nonlinear nonreciprocal optical components with either two or three unknown parameters, a task that was previously impossible using standard linear nonreciprocity approaches. This is achieved by adjusting the coupling point, pump gain, or both to coincide with the critical coupling condition of the signal or idler modes. quantum computing. To bring this technology to practical viability, it is essential to detect and mitigate material defects that cause decoherence. In this study, we employ terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) to examine the local dielectric characteristics and carrier densities of wet-etched aluminum resonators on silicon, a fundamental component of superconducting quantum processors. Leveraging a newly developed vector calibration method, we derive THz permittivity from spectroscopy conducted near the microwave feedline. By fitting the extracted permittivity to the Drude model, we determine that silicon within the etched channel exhibits a higher carrier concentration compared to buffer oxide-etched silicon, and we investigate post-processing techniques to lower these levels. Our findings demonstrate that near-field THz analysis offers a quantitative approach to evaluating and pinpointing loss mechanisms in quantum devices. This remote sensing technique probes a region roughly 100 micrometers above the sample surface, allowing for the detection of features far smaller than the resonator footprint, thereby enabling non-destructive defect characterization suitable for integration into advanced quantum processors. Furthermore, the method is non-invasive and provides permittivity measurements in environments optimal for superconducting quantum devices—specifically, low temperatures and magnetic fields. Near-field optical spectroscopy within the Terahertz range is anticipated to play a crucial role in advancing quantum computing technology. Notably, this approach is adaptable to other quantum systems exhibiting resonant behavior in the microwave to millimeter-wave spectrum, such as spin ensembles. Our work further details a custom near-field optical probe designed to ensure reliable and reproducible measurements across a broad spectrum. in commodity futures, witnessed rising transaction costs following the 2008 financial crisis. These costs are partly driven by prediction error variance caused by autoscaling computer trading systems. The mechanism for autoscaling involves a 24/7 order book with a fixed $25 width; when demand shifts or volatility rises, the price range expands to accommodate it. While this approach benefits the CTA and market makers, it imposes higher transaction costs on smaller participants with limited resources. To address this, Frank Keener and the author previously proposed "micro-micro" trading as a cost-effective alternative. This paper expands on that methodology, examining how a micro-micro trader can execute trades despite discrepancies between predicted and actual demand or volatility. It explores whether cost savings remain possible when small traders experience prediction errors while large traders do not,反之亦然. Additionally, we propose a strategy for micro-micro traders to execute during periods of unexpected demand surges or volatile price shifts, ensuring performance remains viable even when large traders encounter prediction errors and the market is inaccessible. Finally, we illustrate how to estimate a system's scalability using historical time series data of volatility, volume, price, and transaction counts. To simulate micro-micro trading, we developed an R package ("mmicr") that functions independently of specific demand or volatility models, thereby enhancing simulation capabilities. A corresponding package in C++ ("mmicr_cpp") parallelizes the R version for execution at CTA speeds, enabling the simulation of both large and small commodity futures traders. The packages are accessible at https://github.com/rmicr/mmicr/. Our proposed tools facilitate the estimation of transaction costs for various traders within specific market conditions, offering an affordable and effective solution for smaller commodity futures traders. This enables these participants to remain in the market even when transaction costs become prohibitive under high volatility and high volume, which was previously unfeasible when transaction costs exceeded the profit from individual trades. Ultimately, these instruments provide a mechanism to lower transaction costs for smaller CTAs.

This challenge is significant because relying solely on isolated features, such as port numbers, is insufficient for reliably distinguishing application layer protocols. Consequently, dynamic detection methods have emerged. This paper examines the dynamic protocol detection mechanisms utilized by prominent open-source network monitoring tools. Using HTTP as a case study, we demonstrate that all evaluated detectors exhibit limitations, including performance issues, scalability constraints, and vulnerabilities to protocol evasion techniques. Our analysis underscores the need for enhanced detectors that offer greater robustness against protocol-specific traits and the ability to handle high-concurrency traffic. The dataset required for this study, which includes over 10 million HTTP requests, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/mwmuell/nrd. This resource supports rapid protocol detection evaluation in both user space and network drivers, allowing researchers to compare techniques across various protocols, network layers, and monitoring scenarios. The dataset was developed in collaboration with the IEEE Security and Privacy 2021 paper, "An Open Dataset for HTTP Fingerprinting," which provides a comprehensive foundation for evaluating modern protocol detection techniques, thereby accelerating the creation of practical solutions for this difficult problem. We urge other researchers to leverage this dataset and its associated code to contribute to the field of protocol detection.
